NOTICE TO THOSE ABOUT TO PURCHASE FURNI- TURE OR UPHOLSTERY FOR HOME USE OR EXPORT. Ladies and gentlemen about to purchase furniture, whether a single article or a complete houseful, will be well repaid by a visit to URQUHART AND ADAMSON, the well-known cabinet makers, upholsterers, and bedding manufacturers, of Liverpool. Their stock in all the leading and fashionable styles is by far the largest in the North of England, while, what is of more consequence to the purchaser, everything is of guaranteed ex- cellence, although the prices, instead of being higher, are in most instances lower than those often charged for inferior articles. Great attention is also paid to the details of design, on which the appearance of a room so much depends, and truly artistic furniture is produced at the most economical figures. • One great advantage in dealing with this firm is the fact that should their vast stock not contain any article sought for, spe- cial designs will be made and submitted without any charge whatever, so that purchasers may rely on obtaining just what they want. Yor the convenience of purchasers residing at a distance and others not able to call, an efficient representative will wait on them. Goods for conveyance by rail or sea are carefully packed without extra charge, and, if required, experienced fit- ters will attend to unpack and fix things in position. Every facility Is afforded to residents in the country to select goods suited to their wishes without inconvenience, while the saving effected by purchasers is incontestible. In the Bedding li-partnient the greitest care is exercised to use only perfectly purified materials. "Hints on Bedding" (2nd edition) is now ready, and will be forwarded free on ap- plication. A large stock of iron and brass bedsteads is also on view. Woven wire spring mattresses of the best makes only are supplied to fit all bedsteads. THE GODMOTHER'S GIFT. Beside the baby's cradle She sat the whole night long. To lay upon his little lips The kisses six of Song. "This is the kiss shall make him long To drink," she softly sighed, "The fount of Beauty with the thirst • That ne'er is satisfied. "This is the kiss shall ope the eye And stimulate the brain To see what others never saw , And he can ne'er attain. "This is the kiss shall charm his lips So that his whole life long, There honey-bees of thought shall hive The stinging sweets of Song. "And here the kiss of Wandering I print on feet and breast, That he may for possession have , Desire and unrest. "And this shall be the kiss of Love, His life to consecrate To her that shall be lost too soon, Or be found out too late. "These are the kisses five I give My baby in his sleep; The sixth, and sacredest of all, A little while I keep. ":And he shall never know, or, known, It never shall be told, Which sweeter is—the kiss I give, Or the kiss that I withhold." ....Leeds _Mercury Weekly. tiarittte' 5.

A mulatto is a mulatto, and a quadroon is a quadroon, with just one- half and one-fourth of negro blood respectively; and anybody who has once lived in at ex-slave-owning country can pick out the proportion of black or white elements in any particular brown person he meets with as Much accuracy as the stud-book shows in recording the nedigree of famous race-horses. Black and white produce mulattos—all mulattos alike, to a shade of identity;' mulatto and white produce quadroon—all quadroon, and no mistake about it; mulatto and black produce sambo ; quadroon and white give us octoroon; and so forth ad infinity?». After the third cross persistently ' in either direction, the strain of which less than one-eight persists becomes at last practically indis- tinguishable, and the child is "white by law" or "black bylaw." as the case may be. without the faintest mirk of its slight opposite intermixture. I speak here of facts which I have carefully examined at first hand; all the nonsensical talk about finger-nails and knuckbs, and persistence of the neer° type for ever, is pure unmiti- gated slave-owning Prejudice. The child of an octoroon by a white man is simply white; and no acuteness on earth, no scrutiny conceivable would ever discover the one-sixteenth share of black blood by any possible test save documentary evidence. Here, then, we have a clear, physical, and almost =thematically demonstrable case, showing that, so far as regards bodily peculiarities at least, the child is on the average just equally corn. 'pounded of traits derived from both its parents. Among hundreds and hundreds of mulatto and quadroon chil- dren whom I have observed, I have never known a single genuine instance to the contrary. Heredity comes out exactly true; you get just as much of each colour in every case as 7ou would naturally expect to do from a mixture of given proportions. Tin other words, all mulattos are recognisably different from all quadroons, and all quadroons from all octoroons or all sambos.—
ELECTION OF COMMITTEE.

The selection of a committee of twenty members was next proceeded with. Papers, upon which the names of the persons nominated, were handed round, and each one present had twenty votes. ,The , voting resulted ,as follows :—For Messrs. Platt, 21; Blackhurst, 20; Green, 20 ; Barker, 18; F. Monks, 18; Jehn Roberts, 18; J. E. Wright, 17; Skelton, 17; Smethurst, 17; Carter, 15; Jones, 15; Percival, 14; Toll, 14 ; Dobson, 13; Barlow, 13; Perry, 13 ; McCollom, 12 ; Thornton, 12. The above 18 gentlemen were declared elected members of the com- mittee, having received the highest nbmber of votes. Eleven votes each were recorded for Mr. Samuel Davies, Mr. William Diggle, .Mr. R. Isherwood, and Mr. James Morris, and Mr. James Morris and Mr. Samuel Davies were ultimately elected to fill the two vacant places.

I Following on this, We have a minute account of the ' wild animals, the decendants, with modifications, of such as now exist; and the way in Which the writer refers to these supposed modifications shows how familiar he is, not :only with denizens of the forest, but with the doctrine of evolution. Refer- ring to cattle he says When the ancients departed, great numbers of their , cattle perished. It was not so much the want of food .as the inability to endure exposure that caused their , death; a few winters are related to have so reduced ; them that they died by hundreds, many mangled by 1 dm. The hardiest that remained became perfectly , wild, and the wood cattle are now more difficult to ap- proach than deer. . There are two kinds, the white and the black. The white (sometimes dun) are believed to be" the survivors of the 1 domestic roan-and-white, for the cattlein our enclosures at 1 the present day are of that colour. The black are smal- ler, and are doubtless little changed from their state in the olden times, except that they are wild. These latter I are timid, unless when accompanied by a calf, and are 1 I rarely known to turn upon their pursuers. But the 1 white are fierce at all times; they will not, indeed, at- tack man, but will scarcely run from him, and it is not i always safe to cross their haunts. i All this is, of course, purely imaginary, but bow real It seems I Another chapter is devoted to the "Men of the Woods," another to "The Invaders," and a third to "The Lake," which, as covering a large portion of the country, forms a central feature of the story. Thus : ' Beneath the surface of the Lake, there must be con- cealed very many ancient towns and cities, of whiah the names are lost. Sometimes the anchors bring up even now fragments of rusty iron and old metal, or black I beams of timber. It is said, and with probability, that 'when the remnant of the ancients found the water gradually encroaching (for it rose very slowly), as they were driven back year by year, they considered that in time they would be all swept away and drowned. But I after extending to its present limits the Lake rose no further, not even in the wettest seasons, but always re- -1 mains the same. From the position of certain quays vwe know that it has thus remained for the last hundred years at least. Never, as I 'observed before, was there so beautiful an expanse of water. How much must we sorrow that it has so often proved only the easiest mode of bringing the 1 miseries of war to the doors of the unoffemling. Yet , men are never weary of sailing to and fro upon it, and I most of the cities of the present time are upon its shore. And in the evening we walk by the beach, and from the rising grounds look over the waters, as if to gaze upon their loveliness were reward to us for the labour of the day. / The second part of the book develops the story-- such, as there is—though as to this the reader who skims the pages for the story will be likely to be disappointed. "Felix Aquila "is the hero, and he , bias some surprising adventures. He explores the , Lake, and we learn that :

The farther he penetrated the more numerous became the waterfowl. Ducks swam among the flags; or rose with a rush and a splashing. Coots and moorhens dived and hid in the reeds. The lesser grebe sank at the sound of the paddle like a stone. A strong northern diver raised a wave as he hurried away under the water, his course marked by the undulation above him. Sedge- birds chirped in the willows; black-headed buntings sat on the trees, and watched him without fear. Bearded titmice were there, clinging to the stalks of the sedges, and long-necked herons rose from the reedy places where they loved to wade. Blue dragon-flies darted to and fro, or sat on water plants as if they were flowers. Snakes swam across the channels, vibrating their heads from side to side. Swallows swept over his head. Pike "struck" from the verge of the thick weeds as he came near. Perch rose for insects as they, fell helpless into the water. With this extract we conclude. The book is one to,. be read and re-read—not as a story, but as the ex- periences or a naturalist who is gifted with imagin- ation. It 18 a matter of course to say that, issued

It was nearly midnight, the doors and window. shutters were all barred, all the lights in the house Were supposed to „he out, the household in be and asleep long ago. But very quietly and cautiously one of the bedroom' doors opened—a light , gleamed forth—then, candle in hand, a slender figure, clad in a pink flannel drassing.„„eown, with black hair streamuig over her, shoulders, and bare feet thrust into pink-slippers, glided along the landing and down the stairs; With a. quick, frightened glance around her, Susan softly turned tho handle of one of the doors which opened out of the narrow pared entrance hall. She crepi into a little den, which Martin called his smoking-room. It waspartly done in joke, as an allusion to the irreclaimable viciousness of its clikaney.-e-sn fir as Anne hies concerned, Martin i Might smoke in any room of.the Imee he pleased. 1 Th„re Iva' a iii ii iin vroi-oWat-ells-Fwe efts' chair, a 1 shabby table littered with account-books, a .Pile of ' newspapers on - the floor, a gun standing in one corner; a tall, old-fashioned bookcase, with glass- doors, took up nearly the whole -of one side of the room. It was crammed with books of all sorts and sims ; and there were books also—mostly worn and I shWOy ones—on rorrghly made shelves over the fire- ; place. On the topmost shelf reposed a revolver. I Susan glanced- round the room, holding the 1 candle high above her head, and displaying her ! finely-formed arm, as the loose sleeve of her dressing-gown fell hock. i " Wl7at an awful lot of books he she muttered. "How in the world shall I ever find the one I want ? " She first examined, the shelves .over the fireplace. There she found " Whitaker'S Almanac," a " Ready Reckoner," " Rarey on Horse-training,", " Mitten's Dictionary," and a set of Routledge'a '.hatidboctiss —"The Sheep," "The Pig," &c.—and "Geology for the Million. ' Disgusted, she turned to the large hook-case. Setting down her candle on a chair close by, she opened the glass doors, and began to explore the rows of her brother's more Valuable books.. "What dry stuff ! " she thought contemptuously. s.• What a waste of money for Martin to, buY, such bez, -et No wonder he wears such tAabby ;coats stnn'emems, and never hunts or goes lo the aces," shs thought- she she ran her fingers over the. baths: tf , % "Origin of Species," Sir John Libbe-ek "Pro-historic 'Darwin's Man, iderbert Spencer's "Data 01 Ethics," and oih".hooks not usually found ,in thi t., library of a smith fernier. On another shelf Axe discovered some treats,ses on scientific agriculture: mixed up with some v.o4umes of Shakespeare:then came a Gazetteer, a Latin pietionary, and Words- worth's poems. ~ Susan paused in despair. 4gb:mose I B.IoX have to wait till to-morrow, and come- eked look for it when Martin is out. But then Anne wili,he abeit the house somewhere, and will wonder when am aftet, and I shan't sleep to-night unless I know :91 certain!'' She took the candle in her hand again and stood on tip-toe to look at the top shelf of the book-case. "There ibis then !" she cried. "I knew he had got it." , With some difficulty she manassed to reach down a fat book bound in' black, a "Legal' =Handbook.," Her eager fingers turned to the index, and _ then rapidly hunted through the pages until she had fOuld the paragraphs she sought. She read them breath- leaslsstWice over, until she felt she thoroughly under- stood their meaning. Susan was no fool, though she sometimes found it suited her purpose to appear one. Rather, she was especially. keen-witted, where her own interests were concerned •, and she had i no difficulty in Mastering the full bearing of the legal information she had - gained. She shnt up the book in triumph. "it is all right then?' I am safe !" • The next mornent she started and shrieked with terror. She had been so much absorbed in read- ing, with her back turned to the door, that she had not heard approaching footsteps. Susan had believed that her brother had gone to bed hours ago,. but he had been sitting, reading, and smoking in the parlour and had fallen asleep in his arm-chair by the fire. The slight sounds which Susan had made in searching amongst his books had awakened him; and be. coming aroused to the fact that somebody was stirring in the house at an unusual hour, he had opened the parlour door and had conic forth to dis- cover who was the intruder in his own especial deli. ' " Susan ! " he cried, amazed; " what in the world do you want here at this time of night ?" I " I—l only wanted a book," she gasped. There was something terrifying to her in this sudden ap- parition of her brether ;in the dim light, the silence of-midnight, he seemed to her a very stern and grue- some flank... ,

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERE'.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERE'.

On the motion of Mr. BLACKHURST, seconded by Coun- cillor WRIGHT, it was unanimously ,agreed that Coun- cillor Platt should be president of the association.—Mr. James -Smethurst was elected vice-preaideot, and Mr. T. Carter treasurer. Mr. H. J. Longton was proposed as secretary, but he declined to stand. Two or threeother persons-were also nominated; but Ultimately the ap- pointment was left over to be dealt with at a future meeting.
THE TOWN COVIsTIL.

In the course of some conversation relative to the coming election, Mr. F. Moron remarked that if they thought that meeting and protesting would have the Slightest influence on the Council they did not yet know that body. It was like pouring water down a duck's back. They might pass whatever resolutions they liked, but, after all, it came to a question of appoint- ment of Committees. The Finance Committee ought to be the controlling Committee of the Council. (Hear, hear.) The Committees brought up the estimates of the expenditure, and the whole matter was discussed in the Council and adopted by the Council. That was the work of the Council, but it was the habit of almost every Committee to exceed the estimates. What they, wanted was a Finance Committee who would refuse toil pass any accounts in excess of the estimates. (Hear". hear.) That seemed to him to be the only way in which they could exercise control, and any Committee which

• •TIIR MINE CAPTAIN." The parlour door opened, and there entered lion of youth and- brightness and, gaiety, which seemed out of harmeny with the dusky room mid antique furniture, and the orave and homely brother and sister sitting at the table. Susan 'Derrick was reckoned, if not the prettiest, yet What She liked still better to be ;called; the ;most atylishi girl in the neighbourhood. , Her features were irreg,ular, she had a wide full-lipped • mouth, a short, turned- up, nose, a warm brown complexion, wavy dark 'hair Snd•Oreat dark eyes, which could languish and sparkle and look things unutterable. Her figure was straight and slender, and would have been perfect in its outlines, if she had -not squeezed, laced, and padded it out of its 'natural beauty. She wore the lop-sided kind of ,hat -so dear to girls of SusaP Derrick's ' sort—a' black 'Velvet ' hat it •Witi, Pith droopingleathers-:La tight-fitting track jacket' end gown, glittering with, black beads. She still con- sidered-herself to be in mourning; but she had,!as was her custom, ravaged Anne's fuchsia bushes and a bunch of crimson blossoms, now half withered, was pinned amidst the folds of cheap black lace which swathed her throat to the chin. "I asked Captain Stambridge to come in and have a cup of tea," began Susan, with a little eon- scions gi,.ggle. There followed her into the room a stout man Of forty, with pale face, small eyes, and large whiskers. He had come courting in his " Sunday best," and so, in his groat-cost with velveteen collar, and carrying his chimney-not hat in his gloved hands, he had as bourgeois an air as Susan herself : while Martin, in his brown tweed suit; and Anne in her plain grey stuff gown; had the unmistakeable look of country folk. • "Captain " Stambridge had a patronising smile as he shook hands with Anne,but he gave a sort of depre- cating, furtive glance at Martin, who had risen from the tea-table and wished him good evening with a stiff little bow. "Won't you shakis'.hadds with me, Mr. Derrick? " he said, rather uncomfortably. "All right. I've no objection if you have none," and Martin,with a grave, unsmiling face, held out his hand. . James Stambritlge, somewhat confused, notwith standing the complacency which beamed from his fat face, then looked about for a place where he Could deposit his hat. First be hesitatingly placed it on the nartow tep of the bureau, from which it tumbled clown immediately, and had to be picked up and smoothed with his coat-cuff; then after find. lug it a resting-place on a chair, he, with much the. same fussy solemnity that he went through the same ceremony every Sunday in the village chapel, took off his gloves and his ;greatcoat, and folded them up, and finally, rather red 'in the face from his exertions, lie seated himself at the tea-table with a little grunt of satisfaction. • Meantime Anne had produced another cup and saucer from a corner cupboard, and poured otittea, while Martin cut bread and ham for their guest. 'lsere was an awkward silence for a few minutes. san giggled a litle, and was very eloquent with her dark eyes; but her brother and sister apparently '',l4ted for Captain Stanileidge to explain the meaning of his presence there; and by-and-by the fact that this was expected of him, penettated his dense nature. -" We've been having • a serious talk together this l'tening, me and Miss Susan, and the long and the snort of it is, as I may say without any circumlo- cution" (Captain Stanabridge dear'y loved a long word), ' that she has consented to make me a happy man as soon as ever I can get my house in apple-pie order for her. There's a new Brussels carpet with a pattern of roses on it as I was thinking of buying for the parlour, and a few other little ornamentations--"

" Oh, Captain Stanibridge," murmured Susan, letting her long black -•eye-laelies veil her sparkling eyes, "I don't think I went so far as to say that." "Oh, yes, you did, my dear; you said before Christmas, at any rate. But that's what the ladies always do, keep up a pretence of being unwilling—a sort of procrastination, as I may say, don't they now ?" and he turned smilingly to Anne. "Really I don't know," she answered rather coldly. "Well, no, to bo sure; you have had no ex. perience, ma'am—it is not experimentally known t 6 you, if I may so express myself," he replied, in a tone of condolence. "Hadn't we better keep to the point?" Martin broke in abruptly. "You wish me to understand, I suppose, that you and my sister Susan are engaged to toe inarried.h "Just so, just so, Mr. Derrick." Stambridge's small eyes blinked a little under Martin's frown;. "and I hops that as me and Miss Susan have come to a isßfeet and complete understanding and compre- arrsion. You have_po obh1•41,911 to. make, sir." ll= Stambridge scenieti loqinek up e;;If.:70-10 14ot Martin with a sort of defiance. I have no occasion to tell 'you, Mr. Derrick, that I am in a position to support a wife in comfort, I may even go so far as to say luxury—but what is far more important, and vital, and essential to my case, I have the respect and confidence of my neighbours and them as is about 'flicre's nobody in this place, where I have been born andPdni; from my earliest infancy, as can ri,ghtly east a stoneiroe7"-- _ While. Stanibrhige was speaking, Alillo had grow?i very pale, and was looking at her brother with an anxious, eager face. lie gave her no swift glance, as if to reassure her; then he turned to his guest and said, coldly and steadily, "Quite true, Captain Stem. bridge. And no doubt Susan fee.Y.s honoured that you arc willing to marry her—altilkough she has the misfortune to be my sister." "Oh, Martin, don't talk like that l"" cried Susan petulantly. "I don't know what you mean, or what you are talking about." "Captain Stambridge knows what ; mean, though. answered Martin., with a Sombre faosz- ' "We'll let bygones be bygones, if you pleaQ# Mr Derrick," and the other man moved uneasily in ,hi; chair. " This isn't a pleasant way to be talking befor.l the ladies. lam sure lam the last man to wish cast up anything against my future brother-in. law, as is to be. Let bygones be bygones, if you please, Mr. Derrick." "Certainly. I have no objection,if you have none," Tas Martin's cold reply. And no objection to me and Miss Susan making A match of it either, I hope ? " and Stambridge gave an unctuous 'smile in the direction of his be. trothed.

"Noe whatever. Susan is oli enough to know her own mind, and to manage her own affairs." • "Not so very old, neither," pouted Susan. "You aren't as polite as you might be, Martin." " Because I should not feel justified in taking such a solemn and important step without asking your consent, Mr. Derrick," Starnbridge went on in a pompous tone,' "you being the head of this home- hold, and the lawful authority as is your sister's duty to obey." Martin shrugged his shoulders with a sardonic smile. "I don't think you will get either of my Sisters to agree with you there. However, my free and full consent is yours, if you care to have it." The conversation flowed more smoothly after this. Martin, indeed, said not another word but he was careful to keep on replenishing his guest's plate and tea-cup. Anne exerted herself to talk, and Susan smiled, and blushed,and dimpled and prattled. and altogether riveted still more firmly the Chains in which she had bound James Stambridge. " rt, was such a sweet pretty sunset, this evening;" she guthell. "We saw such a great big shooting: star, just after it had got dusk._ I declare it re- minded me of the fireworks at the Crystal Palace,. only, of course, it wasn't nearly so good. Did you ever go to the Crystal Palace, Captain Stambridge ? Dear, how awfully nice it is you should be called Captain! Sounds quite military, don't it? Ido so, dote on the military, as _somebody says in a novel once read." _ _ _

" [shall get jealous if you go talking like that." and her lover looked at her as if not quite pleased, and as he looked, a strange thing happened. As if a sudden recollection had flashed across her, Susan's eyes fell, and the blood rushed crimson into het face. She pushed back her chair from the table, and she began to fan herself with her handkerchief. "How hot the room is," she said pettishly. And' then she began to talkin a hurried voice as if trying to hide her confusion. "It is cold enough out of doors, though. We are going to have a hard winter; there are such lots of hips and haws in the hedges—" " What rubbish people do talk," muttered Martin, , "as if the blossoms which came out last spring' and the berries they turned into this autumn, eon/461feet the winter that:e coming. .

Mr. BRUNNER, MT.., who was introduced as the " hero orNorthwich," was received with a prolonged outburst. of cheering. Noticing the fact thet the room in which be was standing had heen'built byet weavers' union, he spoke of the action of 'the 'Government towards trades , 'unions in England years,agoean'dsaid he wished to ex- , Plain that the chief pert of the policy of the present Government was directed againet an Irish trades union, for the National League was nothing but a trades union of the farmers of Ireland. Wieked things had been done in England, and they knew It. `Wicked things had been done id Ireland, and he assurer them the 88 Irish mem- bers were no more gilltyof the wicked things which had been done in Ireland than Ms 'listeners were of what had been committed in England. "But think of the difference in the policy. Compare what•was done years ago when Broadhead comenttted his -murders in Sheffield, with that which was teing- done by their authority in Ireland to-day. The Govern- ment knew perfectly! well that the relations `betwee! landlord nod tenant in Ireland were in a thoroughlyam- satisfactory condition; that if they had brought in -whin , et the beginning of the session to alleviate the bitterness that existed betvreen landlord and tenant, he did•not'be- lieve thiwtheernries themselves would have considered t here wasany reason whatever for passing a Geercion'Bill. Mr. Chamberlain was ine emeleway the cause of the election last 'year; Ilia obeectioreto Mr. Giadsthne's proposals was that they did notemitate closely enough the Canadian 'Constitu- tion. fie ' (Mr. Brunner) had recently been in,Oatiadae and had seen the working of the Canadian Constitution —the North America Act of 1867—and he assm,ed!them that the North America Act gave a great deal mire Home Bale than Mr. GlacLatone's proposals. Prince Alexander of Battenburg arrived at Dover. on Monday, from Ostend, and proceeded to London. The French Consul at Laurium has been dismissed from his post for having accompanied one of the Princes of the Orleans family on a tour through Greece. Alderman De Keyser, the, New Lord Mayor of London, is not, after all, as has been affirmed, a Roman Catholic. I At any rate the Weekly Register contradicts the report. West Kent has seen the unusual phenomenon of a lady acting as registration agent. At Dartford Mr. A. S. Dixon, who represented the Liberals, was assisted by his laughter. rsh is estimated that 15,000 operatives engaged in tit South Staffordshire and East Woree.sterehire nail trade have now ceased work. The men demand an advance of wages which the employers consider excessive. Reuben York, a yeah, who was engaged with his father, slack washing, on the premises of the Nunnery Colliery Company, in Cricket-road, Park, Sheffield, fell Into the hopper while the buckets were revolving and met with a shocking death. • DISTRESS AMONG 'ME Cornerev'C LRR OT. —The Queen has given E.llOO to the special fund which is being raised by the Corporation of the Sons of the Clergy for the re- , lief of the (listless which exisesso extensively among the ,conntry clergy. The fund, which•now amounts to over 08,000, was started and 'is 'being administered by the corporation in response to Winter which was addressed to the governors by the Archbishop Of Canterbury. THE 'DRIViT I'sWSLRY iiOIII3RRY ra GLASGOVL—On Saturday morning five persons, including a jeweller named Thomas Walker Crawford, Who has an establish- ment in Argyll-street, 'Glasgow, were remanded on a chargeof receiving. Since 'the great jewelry robbery in Glasgow 'the police have been 'very energetic, and the tebing.of a nuniber of Platearesulted in the apprehen- sionofthese five. This is the second batch that has been takeninto custody. _ .

TNERIBLE TRAGTMY TN 'BIRMINGHAM.—Late on Satur- day might rHenry Clews, vroiking gilder, of Hay Mill, near fFirrningham, .quarrelled with his wife over money mat- ters, and struck her on the eye. In retaliation she struck trim ontheside of thelleallwith the knob end of an iron poker,'fracturing the skull. The man fell to the ground stunned, and before medical assistance arrived he was; dead. The woman, on 'finding what she had done, was .diseonselate,.and gave' herself up to the police. _ _

BOARD OF TRADE IRETUREs.—The Board of Trade re- turns issued on Friday show that the value of our im- p-Ash-I thsmonth of September was £27,191,594, against .g 28,898,505 in 1886, and "t 29,863,788 in 1885. The esti- mated 'value of the foreign exports was £4,553,464, against '£44)36,979 in'lBB6. and £5,086,052 in 1885. The value of British and 'lrish produce and manufactures exported in the month was £19,833,830, against £18,928,975 in'lBB6, and £18,621,651 in 1885. ScantarTevma EPIDEMIC.—ScarIet fever, supposed to have been imported, is raging in epidemic form at Hor- wich, and -creating considerable alarm. Disinfectants have been' freely supplied, and isolation has been resorted to as faros practicable, but 'without the desired result; and as a last resort the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Whitaker) has advocated the closing of the elementary schools. 'Opinion is divided as to the advisability of this course, 'and a special meeting of the Local Board will be convened to consider the subject. 'Dmcisrox or larm Cnorreas' Costmisstom.—The Crofters' Commission has Issued decisions in the case of some tenantry in the island of Tires. In 126 cases ortthe Duke of Argyll's estate the Commission has reduced the rental 26 per cent., and has cancelled nearly one-half ,of the arrears owing. A reduction was made in every-case except in that of the President of the local Land' League. In the island of Moss the Commission has made an average reduction in 18 cases of 59 per cent., and all arrears have been cancelled. 'Tam' Ft.oonitro or A WARWICKSHIRE MINF..—At Ex- hail one of the best in the Warwickshire coal- field, which has for months been stopped owing to the extraordinary influx of water into the shaft, great efforts are being made to stop the inflow. Water has been pumped out at the rate of over 1,000,000 gallons every 24 hours,,and the shaft has been emptied to a depthi below where it flows in. Efforts are being made to keep the water back, and it is believed the difficulty will he overcome, and employment again found for the colliers. Tam Bor.Torr STRIKE.— A letter has been received by the Secretary of the Bolton ltatepayers' Association from Abe Home Secretary in reference to contentions laid before him by the deputations who saw him recently in ' London and complained of the action of the authorities In taking extra police into the town to rape with the rioters and to guard the imported -men. The Home Secretary, having given the question the fullest con. sideration, sees no reason whatever to complain of the action of the authorities, and does not consider any in. quiry necessary. The strike hands and their friends are disappointed at the character of the reply. Tam Trrmg WAR: SEIZURES or STOCI.—The tithe war has extended into Monmouthshire, seizures for arrears having been made in the parishes of Ponthir Llantar- mam and Llaniddewi Rliydderch. The goods seized by the bailiffs have been disposed of privately. In another ••casei it. is stated that the tithe-owner has seized and entered upon possession of two fields in the occupation of the tenant. What is probably meant is that the tithe- ownethas seized the produce on the two fields, which he is holding pending its removal. The farmers express their 'determination not to pay tithes. PANIC 'AT A CONCERT.—At A crowded promenade con- ..cert at "Aston Lower Grounds, Birminghanlo.on Sunday evening. one of the.audience in the great hall fell down in a fit, and a commotion ensuing, someone raised a cry of "Fire,"-with the result that a rush was made for the exitsolv number (if people were knocked down, and many “women fainted, but confidence was restored in time to prevent any serious results. The man who raised the alarm got away, hut left his coat in the hands of a per- son who tried to detain him. The audience numbered '7,000. A THEATRE PERRnir ()RIM' CLOSED.—The question of • the license ' West Bromwich Theatre has wain come beforow full bench of magistrates. A full report by the • borotrgh surveyor' was presented dealing with twelve • points, on each of. which alterations were recotnmended. 'The Bench said the fact was that there was only one exit from the gallery, and the construction of the stair- cases ins so objectionable that a license would be re- fused. The undertaking given on granting the provi- sional license last week must be carried' out, and the .theatre closed at once.' _ .

DESPERATE PoAcmso AFFRAY.—at the County Police Court at Shrewsbury, on Saturday. Frederick Little- :hales, Thomas Jones, and William Medlicott were charged with night poaching and assaulting two keepers, named :Boast a and Hart, on the night of the 6th inst. The keepers, whose heads were bandaged, gave evidence of identity,•and the prisoners were remanded for a week. The poachers were discovered laying the nets about mid- night, and they attacked the keepers with large stones and .esoaped. The keepers were very seriously injured, and ,were- taken to the infirmary.

WAHIDO " run WUONG }3ODY.—An extraordinary in- cident has happened at Ayr. Charles Reggans, an Irish- man, died-suddenly in the hospital, and while his body lay in the mortuary which adjoins the hospital his friends proposed to hold a wake on his remains. They .sent James Scullin for the, corpse, but through some mis- understanding he took the ' body of an aged pauper woman instead of Reggaris, and conveyed it to Reggan's house, where'Reggan's father kissed it, and the " w ake " was commenced. Subsequentiy the mistake was dis- nevered, and inquiries led to An explanation, the body eventually lbeing returned to the mortuary. Reggan's body was 'then recovered, and the " wake " proceeded with.

DifiTORBANCE AT Lowysrorr.—A serious disturbance occurred at'Lowestoft on Sunday, in connection with the visit ,of two Socialists, named Nicoll and Houghtm, from Norwich. 'For several Sundays meetings held by Socialists have•been disturbed, and yesterday before the speakers could begin a crowd of 1;000 persons set upon them. Sticks were used, and Nicoll •received a wound on the face. The police escorted the two men to the railway station atnid the yelling and hooting of the crowd, and they-were conveyed to the next station by special train. +People who were suspected of sympathis- ing with the Socialists were illtreated and-hustled.

MALPRACTICER IN A LOAN OrricE.---Hatniltort Miller, late secretary of a loan society in Liverpool known as the City and County Finance Company, was charged on Monday at thetbiverpool Police Court with conspiracy and embezzlement It is alleged that Miller obtained extensive advances fm the cashier on 11,0 ,U's, and that Mr. Allonby, chairmawof the directors, on 'being informed of this practice, commenced with him to obtain similar advances, instead of stopping the irregular practice. After a time Mr. Allenby disappeared, and was then in- debted to the society in considerable sums. The prisoner Miller was remanded. THE NEW CRUISER AusritALta.—The official steam trial of the belted cruiser Australia, built for the Govern- ment by Messrs. Napier and Sons, Glasgow, took place On Friday on the measured mile between the Nore and North Foreland, with most satisfactory results. The engines are those known as the triple expansion type, and the boilers are worked at the very high pressure- -60 fax as marine boilers are concerned—of 1301 b. to the square inch. An ample 'supply of steam was generated without the slightest appearance of priming, while the bearings kept very cooL The mean average speed of the vessel was 188 knots, and the mean indicated horse- power 84876, being nearly 400 horse-power beyond that contracted for. The trial was regarded by the officials as a complete success. FUNERAL OF VIE MURDERED VICAR.—The funeral of the Rev, William Meynott Farley, vicar of Cretinghatn, who was murdered by his curate on Sunday morning last, took plane on Friday afternoon in the churchyard of that parish. Many residents from the parishes around were present, together with several of the neighbouring clergy. The eortige left the vicarage at two o'clock, the 'body, enclosed in an unpolished oak coffin, being con-, veved upon a bier drawn by a pony. Mrs. Farley, the wiabw, was the chief mourner, and there were also pre- sent three sons of the deceased and two daughters. The burial service was read by the Rev. M. Allen, of Winslow, in the church and at the graveside. Mrs. Farley was visibly overcome with grief, and the ceremony altogether was very sad and impressive. The deceased was in- terred close by his second wife, who died in 1881. Soli- citors representing both the accused curate and Mrs Farley were in the village during the day.

?jr. Wm. O'Brien, Kr., has returned to Dublin from London.
Iti stated that the-Irish conitabulary are to be sup- plied with pocket eAmeras. - Mr. Dann states that his main business in visiting America is connected with woollen manufactures.
Archbishop Walsh has sent the Rev. Robert Murphy, parish priest, for the assistance of the evicted tenants at Boxlyke, £25 from the fund which he received from the Irish at the Cape. _ . _ . .

Intelligence rreached Dungannon, on Monday, that as Seven men were putting off from the shore us a boat, on Sunday evening, at Coney Island, Lough Netth, the boat capsized, and five of them were drowned. The men were from Lurgan, on a pleasure trip. An immense number of people assembled in boats to bold a National League meeting, at the confluence of the F Suir and Barrow, on Sunday. The river was black with boats, and the meeting was 'undisturbed by the police. Resolutions condemning coercion were passed. A suspended Roman Catholic priest, named Cash, who, was stated by: Mr. Dillon, M.P., in his evidence at the Mitchelstown inquiry, to have been beaten by the police in the barracks, after the recent fatal affray, was found dead on the roadside near Mitchelstown on Saturday. Mr. John O'Connor, M.P., speaking at Buckfastleigh on Saturday night, stated that after his return from prison in 1881 the Irish officials sought to implicate him in an attempt to murder a judge. The informers were to get men to undertake the task, and Mr. O'Connor, wherever he might be, was to be arrested on a charge of being implicated. The plan, however, broke down, owing to the Government officials and the informers disagreeing.

Meetings of suppressed branches of the National League were on Sunday held at Kanturk and the pro- claimed district of Dubenow. The police were present, and counted the members on entering, but the doors were shut and the meeting held. An unusually large meeting assembled at Kanturk, despite the presence of a considerable body of police, who took the names of all entering the roam. The head constable, who entered, was compelled to leave. _ _ _ _

Thirty-three horses belonging to the hunting stud of Captain Seed, of Clonsilla Park, near Dublin, were found poisoned on Monday. The animals were fed on Sunday night, and had been locked up in their stableshv a groom. The whole stud Were found suffering next morning from the effects of poison, three being dead. and ten have since died, despite the utmost efforts of the veterinary surgeons. Four more horses, including a splendid entire horse, died yesterday. The viscera of the dead animals are being analysed by Sir Chas. Cameron.

Meetings of branches of the National League were held in several of the proclaimed districts of county Cork on Sunday. At Macroorn a meeting, the largest ever known in the district, was held in a private house un- known to the police, and the ordinary meeting of the League was also held. A meeting was held at Rathduane, five miles away, under the presidency of the local Poor. law Guardians. At Carriganima, between Mill-street and Maerootn„ two meetings were held on opposite hill-sides. policemen were present, but did not interiere. THE Mat`CHELSTOWN Titeoxur.—When', the Coroner's Courqaasembled on Wednesday morning, Mr: Harring- ton complained that the extra police—including the in- culpated constables—had been ordered away from the town. The Coroner said. this was a very improper and a highly illegal and unconstitutional proceeding. Mr. Harping-On next addressed the jury, and the coroner having summed up, the jury retired to deliberate at seven o'clock on Wednesday evening, At half-past nine they brought in a verdict of wilful murder against Mr. Brownragg .and five members of the constabulary, and the Coroner issued warrants for the arrest of these per- sons.

ARREST OF CAPTAIN HAMILTON AND EMERGENCY MEN ORDERED.--The inquest on John Kinsella, who was shot near Coolgreany in the affrays' with emergency men, was resumed on Wednesday, at Ballyfad. The Jury, after an hour's deliberation, returned a verdict that the de- ceased John Kinsella met his death at Croghan Middle, on the 28th of September, from a;-gunshot wound felo- niously, wilfully, and of malice aforethought, inflicted by George Freeman, aided and abetted by Captain Ed- ward Hamilton and ten others. Wartants were now issued for the arrest of Captain Hamilton and four others, making twelve prisoners in all. The coroners on the application by counsels said he had no power to ad- mit to bail. THE MURDER OF A HEAD CONSTABLE.

The magisterial examination of the seven persons charged with the murder of Head Constable Whelehan was concluded at Ennis; on Saturday, with the reading of the depositions. Michael and IVer Murphy positively asserted their innocence. The solicitor for the defence asked that bail might be allowed, but th- Bench stated that this was out of their power, and the prisoners were formally committed for trial.

THE DUBLIN CORPORATION AND THE POLICE. On Monday, at a meeting of the Dublin Corporation, Alderman Dillon moved that the action of the police, in refusing to permit the civic sword and mace to be placed before the Lord Mayor during the trial in the Police Court last Thursday, should be referred to a Com- mittee of the whole Council. An old charter of Henry IV:s reign gave power to the Dublin Corpora- tion to ,carry the sward and mace before the Mayor wherever they went in state. Councillor Dawson seconded the resolution and said that as great an insult was offered to the Crown as 16 the Corporation. _ Counc?llor Sexton, a Conservative member ,said that a great indignity was offered to the Corporation by not allowing the civic emblems to be placed before the Lord Mayor. Councillor Kennedy, M.P., Paid summonses should be taken out against the police officers. The resolution was strleintori

div.head: INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY CONCERT.
div.p: INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY CONCERT.

Warrington Public Hall was crowded on Satur- day evening, when the annual concert in aid of the funds of the infirmary and Dispensary was given by a number of popular artistes. The chair was occupied by the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere). The vocalists, who all earned the favour of the vast audience, were Miss Jennie Owen, Dr. Smith, Dr. Luigi Mod, Di. Combs, and Mr. Alfred Cavanagh. Mr. R. W. Pearson conducted an excellent orches- tral band, and Mr. George Riley presided at the pianoforte with his customary ability. Mr. Corne- lius Furness contributed a couple of recitations in a style that was above the average, and he was de- servedly applauded. At the commencement of the j)roceedings the National Anthem was sung by the vocalists and the audience, Miss Owen and Dr. Mapei taking the sqlo parts. This loyal tribute paid, the CHAIRMAN, who on rising was loudly cheered, made a short, but at the same time a very appropriate speech. In the course of it, he expressed the belief that they were that night going to enjoy a very good concert. They must remember that the ladies and gentlemen who 'were giving their services should have the highest praise for what they were doing in aid of the Infirmary. (Cheers.) There had been some changes in the Infirmary since he had ad- dressed them last. On that occasion he gave statis- tics of the income, tevenne, 'and expenditure of the Infirmary, and he would in passing just say that the income was still flourishing, and the Infirmary and Dispensary were doing a very good work. (leat'. hear.) There had recently been some changes in the 'staff at the Infirmary. They all regretted— and he was sure the committee who managed the Infirmary affairs also remtted—the resignation of •Dr. -Richmond. He had been at the Inhrmary for :over eight years, and -over twenty-five thousand patients had passed through his hands during that time. That gave an average of more than three thousand per annum, which meant a great deal of work. Dr. Richmond had resigned after an hon- ourable career, and his place had been filled by Dr. Smith ,who had come with the highest testimonials. IThey had also got an assistant-surgeon, so that in- stead of one they now had two. That meant more expense, and he hoped the inhabitants of Warring- ton would always look upon the Infirmary as one of th,e first things they should give their money to, and that they would do their utmost for its benefit: (Applause.) Letters of apology, he proceeded to, state, had been received from -Messrs. J. Charlton Parr, Jos. Davies, John White, H. Bleckly, W. Cros- fleld, and James Manson. Referring to the concerts of the previous years, his Worship said that in 1882 the receipts of the concert amounted to £47 7s. 44.; 1883, £6l us. 91d.; 1884, £5l 7s. M.; 1885, £47 14s. 7d.; and in 1886, .£3l 14s. Bd.; making a total of • £239 16s. ld. The subscriptions received since the formation of the Warrington Working Men's Infirm- ary Committee were :—ln 1880, £165 9s. 30.- 1881, £33985. 10d.; 1882, p 363 55. 1883, £422 4s. up.; 1884, £397 13s. 7id.; 1885, £478 13s. 6d.; 1886, .1367 is. Bd.; total, £2,533 17s. 6d.; making an aver- • age per year of .£361 19s. 70. (Applause.) From these figures if would be seen that the Working' Men's Committee had done well for the Infirmary in the past, and they were still doing good work for the benefit of that institution. (Applause.)— The programme. was then proceeded with, and, al- though the audience had been requested not to press for recalls, the applause was in one or two instances so enthusiastic and.repeated that it was impossible to resist the demand. The playing of the band was much appreciated, Mr. Pearson gave an excellent violin solo, and the vocalists were well received throughout. At the close a hearty Vote of, thanks, proposed by the thErsinmerr, was accorded to those who had taken part in the concert, and the• Mayor was also thanked for presiding, on the motion of Mr. JOHN ROBERTS, the energetic chairman of the Working-men's Committee, seconded by Mr. Taos. THE BOLTON t.N. 1•1;. : ARREST FOIL IN TINIID.A.TJQN• „ This strike entered its twenty-Second week; on Winds% and efforts are being made to bring about a settlement, by the re-opening of the open trbitraticn regotiations. The joint committee on Saturday decided to reje,ct Messrs. Threlfalks offer of Is. now, and another Is. whea trade justifies it. It will he remembered that the mee resolved to accept the offer, but the London executive refused its sanction. One of the men's committee, named Scott, has been arrested for intimidation. The Joint Committee of the men have decided the:4 Messrs. Threlfall's men shall not accept the one shilling offered by the firm. The men resolved a fortnight ago to accept a shilling now and another shilling when tradc warranted it, but the Central Executive would not sanction the decision, and the Joint Committee, on Saturday, fell in with that resolution. . _

At the'ilolton Police Court, on Monday, a further case arising from the strike was investigated, the defendant, James Scott, being charged with drunkenness and assaulting a man named Sainworth, an imported work- man at an engineer's establishment in the town affected by the dispute. The evidence wont to prove that tits defendant attacked the complainant with an umbrella, and offered further violence, when a policeman inter- posed and took him into custody. The defendant wished to call rebutting testimony, and the case was accordingly adjourned. f-cott is a member of the men's bothmitted.—

div.head: TRAGEDY AT A RAILWAY STATION.
div.p: THE TRAGEDY AT A RAILWAY STATION.

The Westminster coroner, on Monday, held an in- quest on the body of Arthur Horne, aged 18, printer, lately residing at 97, Corporation-buildings, Cleiken- well, who shot himself under romantic circumstances on the platform of the Charing Cross Metropolitan Railway Station, after attempting to murder his sweetheart. Mr. Horne, father of the deceased, deposed that his son had never threatened to commit suicide, nor was he of a jealous disposition. He was, however, at times irritable. Annie Horne said her brother seemed very angry on the morning of the murder, and she asked him what was the matter, but he made no reply. . . . .

Matilda Horton stated that t;lie met deceased on Wed- nesday, and went for a walk, during which the deceased bought her a ring. They entered the train at Westmin- ster. She alighted at Charing Cross. and the deceased following her she sat on a seat, when Horne fired two shots at her, but missed. He then shot himself in the mouth. They had had a quarrel about an engagement ring which he did not want her to wear, and he told her he would lose his situation on Friday. Other witnes...es stated that insanity ran in the de- ceased's family, and the jury returned a verdict oti °Suicide whilst of unsound mind."

The young girl, Matilda Horton, has had, it is reported, various admirers and followers, and she might, on more than one occasion, have comfortably settled down in life, had she definitely chosen between them. She, how- ever, for the past twelve months professed an unchang- ing regard for the memory of a former lover named Arthur Pothecary, also a young volunteer, whom she used to walk out with more than twelve months ago. He considered that, his affections were unreciprocated, and he shot himself with a revolver. On the girl being examined at the hospital, a strange discovery was made. It was found that she had tattooed on her arms the words, "I love Arthur Pothecary." It was at first thought that that was the name of the young man who had shot hitiaself at Charing Cross, and whose dead body was just about to be brought in, but on an explanation being given, it was stated that that was the name of the former young man she used to go out with, and that the sad end of Arthur Horne was a double tragedy in con- nection with her life. •

div.head: MK. CHAMBERLAIN'S VISIT TO ULSTER. •
div.p: MK. CHAMBERLAIN'S VISIT TO ULSTER. •

Mr. Chamberlain left Birmingham on Monday night on his promised visit to Ulster. The right lion. gentleman, who was accompanied by Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., travelled by the Scotch mail timed to start from New- streetStation at 10 15. A large crowd assembled on the platform, and prior to entering the special saloon earrings which had been set apart for him, he was surrounded by a number of enthusiastic supporters who shook hands with him and wished him God-speed. The right hon. gentleman and Mr. Collings having entered the carriage, there were loud cries of "One word," which were many times repeated with accompanying cheers. The passage across to Larne was very rough; but on landing Mr. Chamberlain was enthusiastically received. At Larne Mr. Chamberlain was met by the president of the Liberal Association and numerous gentlemen from Belfast, to whom he was introduced. The right hon. gentleman was accorded an enthusiastic reception from the crowd which followed him to the hotel, where he was entertained to breakfast An address was pre- sented to him on behalf of the Lame Liberal Association; and in reply Mr. Cirmasitetant said he brought from the inhabit- ants of Stranraer a message of good-will to the people of Ireland, in their hour of trial. During the passage, he had been reflecting that Scotland at one time had at; independent Parliament, which was merged in the Go- vernment of the United Kingdom, by an Act of Union, which Act, if he were to follow an illustrious example, he would call a "blackguard proceeding." (Laughter.; The Act of Union had, in the course of generations, firmly cemented the people of Scotland and England, so that Scotland was now as much a part of the United Kingdom as England itself. So LL might, and must be, with regard to Ireland. (Cheers.) He could under- stand that there had been causes for just complaint in Ireland, and these should be removed; and he believed that they would be retrieved by a Democratic Parlia- ment, whilst the integrity of the Empire would be pre- served. (Cheers.) He was prepared for radical but just reforms, and lie thought the time had arrived when every cultivator might be the proprietor of the land he had tilled; and he was in favour of the greatest exten- sion of local self-government consistent with the integrity of the Empire, the supremacy of Parliament, and pro- tection of minorities. (Cheers.) Mr. Chamberlain arrived in Belfast at 12 p.m. 15, having travelled by special train • from Larne. There waive large crowd in waiting, and upon the right hon. gentle- man reaching York-street Station he was greeted with prolongednd enthusiastic cheers, mingled with a few groans. He at once entered an open carriage, and drove to the County Down Station, a distance of two miles. The day was cold and showery, but the weather did not prevent people from lining the streets in large numbers. Flags were floating from a number of buildings along the principal thoroughfares in honour of the occasion. Mr. Chamberlain was driven along York-street at a slow pace, and when he ,had gone a quarter of a mile ths crowd stopped the horses and took them out of the carriage, which was then drawn by cheer. ing men along York-street, Royal-avenue, and High-street to the station of County Down Railway. The cheers of his escort, which increased rapidly as he went along, were alternated occasionally by " Boobs " from some of the working men who followed. The most vigorous hostile demonstration was by the workmen engaged on the new free library buildings, while at the Ulster Reform Club Mr. Chamberlain was received with cheers and waving of handkerchiefs. He left at 12 30, for Craigavad, the residence of Sir Edward P. Cowan. At the County Down Terminus loud cries were made for a speech, and Mr. Chamberlain responded; He said the _Unionist. party. and .the,..Conservative party had saved, and they were , still doing all that In them lay to ptevent injury to Great Britain and ruin to Ireland. The danger, how- ever, had only been avertel for a time, and it seemed possible that the great issue would once more have to be faced. In that case much depended on the attitude of Ulster. (Prolonged cheers.) If the majortty ol Elio people of Ulster were animaled by the spirit displayed that day, he had no fear of the result. If Ireland, as was said, was unanimous in demanding Home Rule, it would be impossible to force upon Ulster a Government which she distrusted.
under

other miserable dissatisfied, and continually the control and leadership of agitators, who profited by the disturbance they created. What he repudiated and hoped they would reject, was the possibility of submit- ting their intelligence, their orderly and well-regulated life, and their commercial reputation, to the rule of an authority which was to be officered by the men who invented the Plan ofCampaignandpropoundedtheNo-rentManifesto. Ile held that he was justified in asking Mr. Gladstone what he intended to do. He had a right.to ask for an affirmative or negative answer to the question, would he lit any future scheme he might put before the people of the three kingdoms provide for the separate treatment of the province of Ulster or of any portion of the pro- vince ? On the question of Mr. Morley's challenge to him to state the plan by which he would concede to Ire- land asertain extension of the privileges and rights of local government, Mr. Chamberlain said ever since the Round Table Conference Mr. Morley and his colleagues _had been in possession of his mind on this subject. Ho should rejoice in a great and generous extension of local government; but if, as he feared was the case from Mr. Gladstone's utterances, it was intended to seek a settle- peat on the principle of a distinct nationality for Ire. hand, that was a scheme for separation and absolute in- dependence, and nothing else.

A fine of 2s. 6d., including costs, was imposed.—James Smith was fined 55., includ- ing costs, for a similar offence.—Mr. Shearer proved the cases.

div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 15, 1887.

MB. CHAMBERLAIN hasn't improved by his visit to Ulster; through being amongst the Orangemen lie has taken an orange tinge. He has grown distinctly worse since he parted company with his friends of the Round Table; for his attitude to- wards Homo Rule proposals grows more and more hostile. Fortunately, the worse he gets, the better it is for the Liberal party, ,for his following,
reduced to Mr. JESSE Coma/cos, and a few other friends of the family, has become fine by degrees arrd beautifully less. It is almost a pity he is go-.
ing to Canada-; if he would only stay at home,
and take rope in the way he has done during the • Paat week, he would hang himself before the next tneeting of Parliament. There was a time when Nit CHAMBERLAIN' called himself R HOMO Ruler.

tven when he opposed Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule Bill, he explained that he approved of its Principal while disagreeing with the methods by which it was proposed that the principle should bo.carried out. Nay, so late as the Round Table Conference, he committed himself to the policy of Parliament for Ireland. But now all this is changed; Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has become a Tory of the, Tories. Speaki gat Stranraer, on his way to Belfast, on Tuesday, and referring to the Ulster Minority, he said :—" It is because I do not believe that a Parliament in Dublin would help them in the slightest degree, because, on the contrary, I kit convinced it would be not only dangerous to great Britain, but disastrous to the best interests Ireland, that I am going to Ireland to support tile maintentace of the authority of the law." It i 8 obvious from this that the member for West

--- tirmingharn has either recently changed his mind, °t'' that he has been playing a part, and was op. Posed to a Home, Rule Pdrliament even when speaking of himself as a Home Ruler: He is en- titled, of course, to change his mind ; but if he would maintain a reputation worth having, he must show why he has changed it, and he has not yet done that. But he is not jus- tified in playing fast and loose with a gre4t princi- Ple. The man who aspires to lead the democracy of the 'United Kingdom must be able to speak with

00 uncertain sound. He must not, chameleon- like, change his hue. with,his surroundings—show- ing himself pink *him amongst English Liberals, and orange when amongst Irish Orangemen. If he does, he may get a pat on the back from lords and dukes, and 4her upholders of class privileges, 'lnt the. people will fall away from thim. Mr. CRAMBERLAIN'S latest declaration is one of unmis- takable hostility to a Parliament in Dublin ; and aa the Liberals of England, Ireland, Scotland, and wales have made up their minds that Ireland titaii have a Parliament of her own, they have 11Briceforward to deal with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN as an out-and-out opponent. We have hitherto held that so long as the member for West Birmingham not set his face against the principle of Mr: sTONE's measure he should be considerately tegardecl as one who might yet be satisfied as to etails; but having denied not only his master °tit himself, Liberals can have no further regard kr or trust in him, so far as the . Irish question is e4)lloerned. Still, when he presents anything in the shape of an argument we need not close our IlYee to it; we can examine it and see what is its i_WKlrth. Speaking at the banquet in Ulster Hall, • ge Went into figures at considerable length to show ti!lat the proportion of S 6 Nationalist members of arliament to 107 Loyalists was not a strict repre- Nitation of the opinion of Ireland. Granted that tzhe proportion is in excess of the actual voting— as the Tory returns at the last election ! °tore in excess compared with the actual vot- and how does it affect the issue? Is it Ileum, making every allowance, that a large, a! t‘ry large, proportion of the people of Ireland are 44 in favour of Home Rule? Nothing of the kind; 414(1, happily, we can answer Mr. CHAMBERLAIN by gliuting Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. Referring to the el•ction of 1885, he says :—" Taking the seats in I,,Which there was a square fight between , the i r„,"lienists and the: Pamellites, I find that the votes I ?Wen were 297,000 Pamellites and 80,000 Union- about 31, to 1;. but the members returned 1/7._ere 6,5 to 5, or 13 to 1." That is to say, on the 4".5t showing he can make out for his own view of ;le case, the majority in favour of Home Rule is L gree-and•-a-half 'to one I 'ls that majority not ge enough? What majority, does he want "4at is the use of his talking about his relations the democracy, if when the democracy of a "(kutry are in a majority of three-and-a-hall to Ze their demands are not to be recognised? Will ,r• erremsErtrAlN be good enough to tell us what larger than this, will satisfy him; and ;en he has done that will he inform us, further, h ilat are his hoes of obtaining such a majority as kr"naY name in favour of the Unauthorised Pro- it ainnre ? People who want to some regard to the voice of the people, and, when "fuddle," either at the time of an election or any they find that voice demanding something in' un- other time, should do so at their own expense..mistakeable terms, it is their 'duty to give it due I attention. Lord Dunraven, and other Tory speakers, seem to think that, if the GovernMent display more of the firmness which was shown by the police at Mitchelstown, what they look upon as the tyranny of the National League will soon. be at an end. This is rank Toryism, and there- fore rank folly. The Tories of 1819 justified the massacre of Peterloo after the same fashion; but the action of the authorities at Peterloo has long been condemned by men of all parties, as the con- duet of the police at Mitchelstown will be half-a- dozen years hence. Lord Dunraven reproaches MR. GLADSTONE for accepting the statements of Mr. DILLON and Mr. LABOUCHERE rather than those of the Irish Secretary. But Mr. GLADSTONE had, too, the accounts of Mr. Bars- lila and other eye-witnesses, and surely eye- witnesses are more to be depended upon than the opinion' of a Man who was hundreds of miles away when the affray took place. Mr. BALFOUR was supplied, of course, with official accounts; but, seeing that the officials are implicated, it is not too much to say that their statements ought to be received with caution., The police, SO Ma. There is coercion within the law and there is caution beyond the law. The present Government are trying both, and the evidence is accummulating that their policy—if policy it can be called—is doomed to ignominous failure.

Several persons were fined at Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, for allowing their dogs. ,to be at large contrary to the recent order. It is rather hard on the brutes that they should be muzzled.; but, considering the number of cases of hydrophobia there have been this season, it would be better if some of the dogs were destroyed. One human being is of more value than many clogs.

IThe feud between the rival bill-stickers of St. Helens is getting to be of a deadly character. As the time of the magistrates has been so much occupied with these quarrels, they are quite right 1 in resorting to heavy penalties by way of ensuring Ithat the luxury of fighting shall be costly. These bill-stickers, if they are left to themselves, will be 1 in danger of becoming man-stickers.

Sir A. B. Walker is now married again, and we may all wish him and Lady Walker much happi- ness. ' One of the mottoes at Okeover was—" May their home be a house of peace." Considering that they have two large mansions—one at Gateacre and another in Derbyshire—they are more likely to have a house of peace than those who begin with a piece of a house--7and a mother-in-law.

The present Administration has earned the title of the Madcap Government. It has forged chains for Ireland, and now it cannot put them on. Irish- men are everywhere laughing at the failure of "the Castle" to lay hold of Mr. O'Brien and the Lord Mayor of Dublin. The attack upon the National League has thus far strengthened it; new members are being enrolled by hundreds. Really, the League ought to pay the Government something for advertising it.

Tax Annual Meeting of the United Singdora Alliance was held in Manchester on Tuesday, and it is satisfactory to see that, although Temperance Reformers are conscious that the Irish question has thrust them somewhat in the background, they are full of hope in the present and of pre- paration for the future. One of the speakers had something to say about Mr. GLADSTONE having done nothing when he had 350 members at his back pledged to local option, and it certainly seems as if an opportunity had been let slip. But Eng- lishmen—and Mr. GLADSTONE is an Englishman— cannot occupy their minds with more than one thing at a time; and neither Mr. GrAnsToNE nor any other statesman can change the current of thought when it has set in a certain direction. What temperance men have got to do is to force themselves so completely to the front, that, when the Irish question is disposed of, they may be in a position to say—" Our turn next." They seem, at last, to have realised the necessity of taking a course of this kind. Instead of pressing the question of Local Option bymeans of ,a resolution in Parlia- ment, it was reselved, at the meeting on Tuesday, that a bill on the subject should be brought in the House of Commons. Mr. W. JOHNSTON, M.P. for South Belfast, has undertaken to introduce the measure, which will be immediately framed and laid before the country. In view, of the possi- bility of an election being suddenly sprung on the nation, it is well that this course has been decided on. Meantime the various temperance organisations in each constituency should bestir themselves with a view to obtaining pledges from sitting members, and from candidates anxious to occupy sitting members' seats. There has been not a little negligence in this respect in the past. Why should the electors of Warrington, for in- stance, be in any state of uncertainty as to the opinions of Sir GILBERT GRBENALL and Mr. JOHN' Caosrumn on the temperance question? They r will both say, in general terms, that they are in favour of temperance, but something more is , needed. Temperance men require to know , how far, and in what direction, they will go in order to promote the sobriety of the nation. It should not be left to the Alliance to settle'matters of this kind. It is a duty which clearly devolves upon the local temperance society—a duty which, to speak plainly—has hitherto been shirked, but which, it is to be hoped, will be shirked no longer.

Dr. Dallinger's lecture on Monday evening was a treat of the highest order. How beautifully he illustrated the infinite in little The schoolmen of olden time used to discuss ho* many angels could dance on the point of a needle, and they have been laughed at for their pains. But modern science takes the edge off the absurdity; Dr. Del- linger finds numerous bacteria in a drop of water literally taken from the point of a needle. They are all God's creatures, and who shall say they are not angels P

lln the second number of "The Naturalist's Monthly," a new sixpenny periodical published by Mr. Walter Scott, the Rev. Dr. Dellinger contri- butes the first part of his Fernley lecture. It is characterised by the learned naturalist's luminous treatment, and is worthy of close study. The first number contains a paper on Binary Suns by Mr. Herbert Sadler, F.R.A.S., and a biography, with portrait, of Charles Robert Darwen. Altogether, ' "The Naturalist's Monthly" makes a good start, 1 and is therefore well worthy of support.

The Welsh are bent on the disestablishment of the English Church in Wales; and tie leaders of the Liberal party are ready to aid them. Dises- tablishment in Scotland and in England will fol- low; but the Church need not fear. If her mem- bers are true believers, voluntaryism will keep her alive. At Blackburn on Sunday, the Chapel-street Congregational Church had a collection to clear off the remnant of the debt on the fabric. When the threepenny bits, &c., were counted, it was found that the total sum realised for the day was £1,363. That was something like a collection.

Aubrey Egerton Hall, a junior clerk in a St. Helens Bank, has been trying to live in a Arst- class style on a third-class salary, and, like many a foolish fellow before him, he has come to grief. He owed £5 15s. Od. for luncheons, and, failing to pay on a judgment summons, a commitment summons has been granted. The judge pointedly remarked that it would have been better for him if he had had a penny roll and a glass of milk. Just so, but he wanted to "Keep up appearances." Oh, these appearances—they make fools of millions, and are the ruin of thou- sands.

ILLNESS OF LORD DE TABLEY.—Lord de Tabley lies dangerously ill at his country seat, Tabley House, Knutsford. His Lordship has been in fail- ing health for some time past, but, although feebYe, he has been in the best of spirits. His lordship is at present unconscious, with lucid moments at intervals. • TEE Buy. G. S. REANEY.—The 'Christian World" in a recent issue says :—We should hear fewer com- plaints about the faildre of our churches if we had more ministers like the Rev. G. S. Reaney, of Step- ney Meeting [and formerly of Warrington]. He is a man of singular tact and ability, clear-sighted, and honest, in the fullegt sense of the word. By making it his first object to do.goocl to those about him and to appear to them as their brother rather than their "parson," and by giving heart and soul to his work, he hasinade himself trusted and beloved by a mul- titude of people little disposed to be affected by the ordinary church methods. His success is a con- spicuous example of what may be accom- plished by "sanctified common sense." It is with - peculiar regret, therefore, that we hear that on account of ' the ill-health of his children—and to some extent of his own—re- quiring change of climate, he may have to leave the liast-eud. If this removal has to be made it will leave a vacancy hard. to fill; made much harder to fill• by the fact that Mr. Reaney's work/ is supple- mented to so great an extent by the labours of his gifted wife:

CONGREGATIONAL UNION.—The autumnal meet- ing of the Congregational Union of England and Wales was opened at Leeds on Wednesday, under the presidency of the Rev. Alexander Mackennal, of Bowdon. There waq a large gathering of ministers and delegates. The President delivered an address, the special theme of which. was" The life of the spirit," and in the course of the proceedings a report was presented by the Jubilee Committee appointed at Birmingham in 1880 to raise a special fund for strengthening the church aid and home missionary work of the churches and other purposes, from which it appeared that the receipts up to date amounted to nearly £430,00G. A paper was read on the subject of county conferences for the revival of faith and purity in the churches; and the Rev. Dr. Clifford, vice-president of the Baptist Union, ad- dressed a meeting on the desirableness of a closer relationship between the Congregational and Bap- tist Churches. Mr. Barran, M.P., expressed his belief that, without any sacrifice of conviction on either side, something might be done towards securing closer union between the‘two denominations. The Warrington Congregationalists were represented at the Union by the Rev. J. Youge, Mr. R. Roberts, and Mr. J. S. Garland. " sApo-Lncr," or Linseed Soap, cherishes the cuticle. 6c1., pest free.
