POOR BATE FOR HALTONAA IDWif ate "Of lid, in the E has been laid for Halton. The rate is estimated at £27785.3d.. . . • HOIST ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—Whilst working on a hoist at Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and ,Co.'s works on Monday, William Wainwright, of 9, Albert-road, Halton View, fell a distance of 20 feet. He severely sprained his ankle and leg, and was attended to by Dr. Mc- Donnell.

MISSIONARY MEETING AT FARNWORTR.—The annual missionary services were held at Farnworth Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday, and on Wednesday the public meet- ing took place. Mr. J. Brock, J.P., presided, and speeches were delivered by the Rev. J. Sowerbutts, of Birkenhead, returned missionary, and Mr. T. Robinson. VISITORS TO BLACKPOOL Should stay at the Station Temper- ance Hotel, right opposite Central Station.. Central position. Commodious and accommodating. Terms easy.—Apply J. _ .

FARNWORTH WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—The anniversary ser- vices in connection with this place of worship were held On Sunday, when a sermon was preached in the morning by Mr. T. Robinson, and in the evening by Mr. G. Davies. The collections, which were in aid of the trust fund, were a little lower than they were last year. _ .

; SUDDEN Darn AT Wrzems. Jonathan Neild, a labourer, 62 years of age, of 105, Mersey-road, died sud- denly on Sunday morning. On returning from his work at five o'clock, he complained to his wife that he had felt cold during the night; and that he had a pain in one of his fingers. Dr. Hutchinson was sent for, but before that gentleman arrived death had occurred, it is sup- posed, from heart disease. ReXcoux BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery Office, on Wednesday. Present— W. Littler and R. Morris, with W. F. Salkeld, secretary. The SucretA;ry presented the following report :—lnter- ments for siN months ending September 25th, 157 ; cor- responding period last year, 157. Fees received during , the same period, £173 12s. 2d ; last year, £l5B 12s. 6d. : increase, £l4 195. Bd. There was no other business of public interest. 1 IMPORTANT DISCOVERY RV A RUNCORN GENTLEMAN.— ' Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst, J.P., of Rhyl, formerly of Run- corn, claims to have discovered 'a process by which Sea water may be transformed into a refreshing, effervescing, saline draught. The invention has been patented by Mr. Hazlebarst under the title " Thalassion. ' A discovery like this must prove invaluable to persons shipwrecked at sea, and cast away for days in an open boat without a supply of fresh water. DEATH OF MR. JOHN DAVIS.—It is with feelings of re- gret that we record the death of Mr. John Davies, of Farnworth, and head chemist at Messrs. N. Mathieson and Co.'s works, Widnes. Deceased, who belonged for-1 merly to Glasgow, was an old employ 6 of Messrs. Mathie- son ond Co,. having entered their laboratory soon after the erection of their works, some 16 or 17 veers ago.l Throughout that long period, by his sterling integrity, the faithful discharge of his onerous duties, and his geniality, he has earned the respect of masters and work- men alike. Unfortunately, through a severe attack of bronchitis, he has been debarred from performing his work for the last ten months, and at nine o'clock on Sunday evening he succumbed to this dire disease, in his sixtieth year. FUNERAL OF A FARN*ORTH FOOTDALLER.—At Fern- , worth, on Sunday afternoon, the funeral of Mr. William , Lomax, aged 21, formerly a member of the Farnworth Football Club, took place. Deceased, who resided at Simms Cross, and was employed by Messrs. Muspratt and Sons, has been ailing for past two weeks, succumb- ing to congestion of the lungs, brought on by cold re- ceived in a football match in which he recently took part He was also' a member of the first-class of Farnworth Sunday School. The ceremony was performed in an impressive manner by the Rev. J. E. Lawton, curate of Farnworth, many persons assembling at the graveside to pay a last tribute of respect to the deceased's memory. The members of the first-class males at Farnworth Sun- day School, several of the, deceased's late fellow-em- ploy-es, and the members of the Farnworth Football team together with Miss Hibbert, the deceased's late teacher, and other teachers and scholars of Farnworth Schools were present. •

HATEST FESTIVAL AT WIDNES.—The annual harvest thanksgiving services in connection with simm's Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel, Widnes, were held on Sun- day, when Mr. J. Kendall, of Blackburn, preached morn- ing and evening to large congregations. In the afternoon the chapel was again crowded, a service of song, en- titled "Harvest Echoes," being the cause of attraction. The musical portion was rendered in a very pleasing manner by the Hutchinson-street Primitive Methodist Chapel choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Lewis, the connective readings being efficiently given byltir. Samuel Drought. At each service there was a collection in aid of the Trust Fund, ZS 10s. being realised. On Monday a fruit banquet was held, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Rollason. Addresses were delivered by Messrs. Pincers, Lee, Drough, and Owens, the Hutchinson-street choir again enlivening the proceedings by the rendition of musical selections. There was a good attendance. The room had been tastefully decorated for the occa- sion. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD FINANCES.—A special meeting of Widnes School Board was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. T. S. Timmia presided, and there were present the Rev. Dean Finegan, the Rev. T. Clark, Rev. G. Bond, Messrs. R. H. Davies, R. Bradshaw, H. W. Deacon, F. Heyes,Dr.O'Keeffe, and G. H. Danby-(clerk). The business was to receive the statement of receipts and expenditure by the Board for the half-year ended 29th September. The receipts amounted to £4,495 18s. ed., including a balance of £7OB 3s. Bd. on March 25th, £3,000 from the rating authorities, and £753 Sc. 84. from school fees. The expenditure amounted to £4,509 14s. 44. The principal items were salaries of officers of the Board £323 Bs. Bd., legal and other expenses of ad- ministration £124 19s. Bd., salaries of teachers £2,489 3s. 4d., books, apparatus, and stationery £93 3s. 24., furniture, and repairs to building, &c., £3B2' is. 3d., re- payment of principal and Interest of loans £991 5s LI. The outstanding liabilities of the Board amounted to £32,188 18s. 74. The statement was approved on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe.

COMPLIMENTARY DINNER TO A WTDICES FOOTBALL TEAM.—Mr. John Brock, J.P., managing director of the firm of Messrs. Sullivan and Co., chemical manufac- turers, Widnes, gave a dinner to the fbotball team con- nected -with the works. The primary cause of this generosity was the fact that the team succeeded in win- ning the gold medals offered for competition by the Widnes Football Club for local teams, under circum- stances which are fresh in the memory of the readers of this journal. A capital repast was provided at the Central Hotel, by Mr. Parkes, and altogether about 45 persons were present. The after proceedings, which were presided over by Mr. Minton, the works manager, were of the usual social character. The principal toasts were "Success to the British Alkali Works," proposed by the Chairman and reoponded to by Mr. Says; The health of Mr. Brock," pr:posed by Mr. Bowker, the cap- tain of the team. Bow's were given by Messrs. J. .T. Latham, F. Wilkinson,E. Harrison, Ashall, Hayes, W, Leatherbarrow, and dolt. In conclusion the health of the host and hostess was proposed, and suitably respon- ded to by Mr. Parkes. . . . _

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. - The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Colonel Ashton (presiding), Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Lockwood ; Messrs. Mclntyre, Brandreth, Parr, Hadfield, G. Kirk- ham, Aaron, S. Taylor, Hewitt, Stokes, Lewis, I. W. Kirkham, and H. Linaker (clerk.)—Mr. Hadfield, in submitting the minutes of the Finance Committee, re- ferred to a charge of £I.I for repairing a washing and mangling machine, which the Committee thought was a somewhat exorbitant charge. The Workhouse Master said he had written to the Runcorn firm which made the charge, but they declined to make a reduction. He also mentioned that the machine was a large one, and was used for the whole of the washing of the Workhouse. They could not have bought a new one for anything like the money.—On the suggestion of Mr. Mentyre, Mr. Aaron and Mr. Kirkham were deputed to examine the machine, and on their return, Mr. Aaron said that the machine had been made as good as new, and in fact it was all new except the frame. It was a great deal cheaper getting the repairs done than buying a new machine, which would cost £2o,—Mr. Brandreth called attention to the NO that there were a number of boys at the Workhouse who were qualified to take employ- ment.—. The Workhouse Master said that there would be more boys and some girls ready for employment after the school examinations.—Mr. Mclntyre gave notice that at the next meeting he woutd move that a coinmittee should be appointed to visit the lunatic from the Union at chestier „The reliei eases were next proceeded with.

BRTINSWICIC MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—At the meeting of the members of this society on Wednesday, Mr. J. D. Joni* read a paper in which he ealt with the question of meal option and teetotalism. , HALTON BriniAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was Iheld on Tuesday evening in the girls' school, the Rev. J. Lockwood presiding. The only business of importance was the passing of a precept upon the overseers for £2O, being £lO less than last year's. SERIOIITS CRANE ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.-011 Wednes- day, James Traynor, a labourer at Messrs. Pilkington and Sons' chemical works, Widnes, and a resident of Moss Bank, was admitted into the Widnes Accident Hos- pital, suffering from a fracture to the right collar bone, concussion of the brain, and a slight injury to the back, received by being struck and knocked down by the handle of •a crane whilst at work at the commencement of the week. PRESENTATION TO CHIEF CONSTABLE WOOD.,—OR Wed- nesday, at Widnes Police Court, Chief Constable Wood, of St. Helens, was presented with a splendid gold centre seconds keyless watch, with a gold guard and pendant, as a mark of esteem from the inhabitants of Widnes:

The watch bore the following inscription :--" Presented to Chief Constable Wood, of St. Helens, in recognition of bi Valuable services." Mr. Wood was warmly com- plimented upon the manner in which he, had performed his duties. The gift was suitably acknowledged. FUNERAL OF A WESLEYAN AT WIDNES:—The remains of Thomas Hughes, 49 years of age, whp died suddenly on Friday last week, under circumstanbes already re- ported, were interred on. Monday ,at .Farnworth Parish Church. A service was conducted in Albert-road Wes- leyan Chapel by the ROTA. R. Burdon and J. Bryant, and at the grave side these gentlemeit also officiated. ' The members of the Biblerflas.s, which 4.4 formerly in charge of the deceased, the select class, and many friends of the Wesleyan body, took part in theluneral proces- sion. Numerous wreaths were laid upori the coffin. WESLEYAN MISSIONARY MEETING AT WIDNES:—A pub-

lie meeting in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Mission;was held in Hartland Memorial Chapel on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance, and the chair was occu- pied by Mr. Thomas Whitby, who was supported by the Rev. McKenzie Cobban, Mr. Gnanainuttchu, a Hindoo teacher, and the Revs. R. Bunion and J. Bryant. Mr. Bryant read the annual report, which showed that the income of the society was £128,906 Us. 11d., towards which the Widnes circuit had raised £l4B as. 2d. Of this little amount Hartland Chapel had contributed £l2 Ils. The total expenditure of this society was £134,992 .13s. 5d., leaving a deficiency of £6,086 Is., 6d. Ad- dresses were given by the Rev. McKenzie Cobban, and Mr. Gnanainuttchu, and the usual devotional ser- vices took place. Virnms POLICE NEWS.—On Saturday Mr. T. S. Tim- mis sentenced Edward Godfrey to 14 days' hard labour in default of paying a fine of 10s. and costs for the offence of drunkenness. Ralph McCloy, of Halewood, suffering from mental aberration, was remanded to the Workhouse Hospital. He was wandering about the street on the previous evening, and P.C. Jackson took him under his care. On Monday Mr. Timmis fined John PalM and Wm. Lea, of no fixed residence, and Patrick Burns (aged 16), of Midwood-street, and John Moran, of Elizabeth-street, five shillings and costs for drunkenness. On Thursday, before Mr. Gossage and Mr. Deacon, the following were fined for drunkenness :—Dominic McDonald, John Mulney, Samuel Kirk, Michael Quinn, and Catherine Campbell. For creating breaches of the peace, Wm. Moran, Alice Gavan, Margaret Knockton, Frank Hollingsworth, and Catherine Lancaster were each bound over to be of good behaviour. ' Patrick Dogherty, of Waterloo-road, was fined is. and costs, 45., for allow- ing the chimney of his dwelling-house to be'on fire. RUNCORN CHURCH INSTITUE : OPENING CONCERT.—The first concert in connection with the recently established Church Institute was held in the National Schools on Thursday evening. The audience was of encouraging proportion, and the music was of the higttest class. The principal vocalist was Miss Greenall, who rendered three songs in a style that called forth loud demonstrations of approval, and she was once recalled. Mr. A. Timmins sang " Madeline " with taste and expression, and Mr. Josef Cantor, who gave the humourous sketch "A journey by rail," and a tragic sketch "A Timbuctoo Idisaster," in his usual clever and entertaining manner, again proved himself to be a general favourite. Miss Argent performed several pieces of music on the violin, and Miss Isherwood performed a pianoforte solo. The pupils of the last named lady sang the "Toy symphony' in a pleasing manner, and the Parish Church Glee Class rendered the glees "The hop pickers" and "The village blacksmith." The solos in the latter piece were sung by Miss Howard. Mr. James Wood was awarded an encore for a capitally executed cornet solo. Mr. Garner, Mr. Cavgill, Mr. Cantor, Mr. Pow- nail, and Miss Greenall officiated as accompanists. The proceedings were conducted by the Vicar, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood. FALSE SCALES AND LIORT WEIGHTS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions. on Thursday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Messrs. Lawrinson and Ward, provision dealers, Waterloo-road, were sum- moned for having in their possession two pairs of scales which were uniust.—Superintentent Barker deposed that he visited the defendant's shop on the sth inst. He there , examined a pair of counter scales, and underneath one I of the scales he found a piece of paper, which had evid- ently been placed there fol purposes of fraud. Another pair of scales were two drachms out of balance against the purchaser.—Superintendent Barker proved previous convictions against the defendants, who were further summoned for having a number of light weights in their possession.—Superintendent Barker stated that on the day previously mentioned he found a 7 lb. weight,which was three drachms light; three 4 lb. weights, each two drachms light; a 21b. and a 11b. weight, each one drachm light.—Mr. T. J. Peters, who represented the de- fendants, informed the Bench that it was more the mis- fortune of the defendants than their fault, that they were summoned. If the magistrates punished them they would he punishing them for something they could not avoid. No one would say that the defendants would be personally guilty of fraud, and they adopted every means to prevent such a thing.—The Bench imposed a fine of 40s. and costs'in each case.—William Wray, pro- vision dealer, Waterloo-road, was fined ss. and costs for having a pair of scales which were unjUst.—Superinten- dent Barker said a loose ball weighing 5 ounces was at- tached to the pair of scales.—The defendant stated he did not know it was an offenceto have the ban loose.

'Wilms Film PUBLIC LIIMARY.—The monthly meeting of the committee of this institution was held on Friday afternoon' at the Public Offices, Victoria-square Mr. H. Wade Deacon presiding. The Librarian reported that the total daily attendance during the month of Septem- ber had been 12,458, against 11,921 last month, an aver- age per day of 479, against 441. The total issue of books had been 4,800, against 4,273 the previous month, an average of 184 per day. The total receipts had been £3 Ds. sd.' which included £1 17s. 4d. for fines. The Chair- man stated that Mr. Allen had written to the Local Go- vernment Hoard asking if the committee would be justi- fied in spending £l5 out of the Id. library rate on the provision of Jree lectures, but had received an unsatis- factory reply. The Local Government could not see that the committee were entitled to spend the money for such a purpose. At his request, however, Mr. Allen had written again pointing out what the money was really required for, and he had received a reply stating that the Board would consider the matter. The Chairman explained that the committee were £l2O worse off than what they thought. It appeared that the £l2O of the amount realised by the id. rate, which they failed to ex- pend in the year ending March, 1887, was lost to them. This had come out during the secent visit of the auditor. The money realised by the ld. rate they must spend in the year fbr which it was realised, or lose it. It was stated that Mr. Gossage having passed through the library, and noticed that there was a scarcity of books for boys, had bought 93 volumes of books of fiction and travel, suitable for boys, at a cost of £lO. The thanks of the committee were tendered to him.

FUNERAL SERMON BY THE VICAR OF RUNCORN. At the Church of St. Michael and All Angels, on Sunday last, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, vicar of Runcorn, preached a sermon having special reference to the lamen- ted deaths of Mr. John Hewitt, of Pereivals-lane, and Lieutenant G. F. S. Joule. Taking his text from 1 Thessalonians, IV. 13 and Di verses, the vicar, after a scriptural exposition, said some of those present had lately had friends whom they believed had fallen asleep in Jesus. Let them thank God for that. There was one who for many years had lived amongst them, and who was a thorough Christian, who was on his way to fulfil his duty to God when the word came to him. In a mo- ment he heard the message and answerdd the call. It was painful to die so suddenly ; even to those who were at peace with God and man, as they believed their dear brother—Mr. Hewitt—was. True, he had no opportu- nity to say farewell to those whom he had left; but the loss would only add brightness to his future welcome to them in Paradise. Strong testimony had been borne to his probity and earnestness, and they could not be too thankful that he had died a thorough Christian. The other death he had to refer to was that of a younger. man George Frederick Joule. He was a young man of much promise, well-known and well-liked. In busiimss in recreation as an officer of the Volunteers, as a member of their choir, as one who had often read the word of God in their hearing, he was one to whom men turned for kindness and gentleness, and one in whom when they looked they found those mialities. Whilst not wish- ing to underrate the sadness which was occasionedbythe death, it was to be hoped that his sudden call would be good for himself and good for all of them. It would be good for them if, while their hearts were warm, they prayed God to comfort and support the widow; it would be good for them if they suffered it to stamp on their hearts the certainty of death and the uncertainty of life. It would be good if they learnt to live so as to be prepared for the certainty of death.. As children of a loving father to whom they had a responsible account to render, their religion must not be played with. No, it must be the real thing, and they must see that their souls and spirits were made wholly for good, so that their thoughts of good might interest them in their daily life. It was through their religion that they learnt to say "Blessed are the, dead that die in the Lord." They learned through it how to conquer sin and Satan, and they learned through it to look forward beyond the grave and all the troubles of this world to the life eter, nal, and to a, gloriousgesurrection. During the service the choir sang the anthem "messed are the departefr,b, a most impresgivo maw,.

PROMOTION OF A RUNCORN LIEUTENANT.—The "Lon- don Gazette" announces the promotion of Lieutenant A. 'Timmins a the F Company (Runcorn detachment) of the Earl of Chester's Rifles, to the rank of captain. Cap- tain Timmins is a smart officer, a brilliant shot, and the appointment is a very popular one. THE STONE THROWING NUISANCE AT RIINCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, James Austin, 10 years of age, was charged with throwing stones on the 28th September. P.C. Hamersley proved the case. Superintendent Hollingsworth said he was obliged to take these proceedings in consequence of complaints of win- dows being broken, and other damage to property. It was very unpleasant to the police to summon these small boys, but they had no alternative. The boy was ordered to pay costs, 3s. Bd.—W. Wilkinson, &youth, was summoned for throwing stones in Lord-street on Sunday night, the 2nd inst., and, on the evidence of P.C. , Kettle, he was fined is. and costs, Bs. ed. BRE WE OF BYE LAWS.—Before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Sarah Littlewood, of the Albion IGn, Peel-street, was sum.

mord for not causing to be painted or fisea upon her premises her name, and a description of the business she Wa3 licensed to carry on.—The defendant said her name was now Blackburn and not Littlewood. She had not got the name painted on the sign, as she was thinking of leaving the place, because she had lost £4O during the past year. Her name and business was now painted on the premises.—P.S. Woolley proved the case, and Supt. Hollingsworth stated that it was in Consequence of the repeated alteration in the name of the occupier of this house that he obtained the order under which the sumrtions was issued.—A fine of 10s. and costs was im- posed.

- - -- FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTION AT RUNCORN.—OR Monday, at Runcorn Police Court, John Jones, Samuel Ellis, Samuel Mather, and Thomas Foulkes, youths, were charged with having, on the evening of Sunday, the 2nd inst., obstructed the footpath in Church-street.— P.S. Woolley proved the case, and the defendants pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Hollingsworth said this offence constituted a great nuisance, and the persons attending the churches and chapels in the town had fre- quently complained. Each defendant was fined is. and costs.—For obstructing the footpath in High-street, on the same evening, Sarah Alice Clarke and Sarah Davies, young women, were also fined as. 6d. and .costs, Bs. 6d. Sergeant Woolley said these women were habitual offenders, and it was of not the slightest use the police speaking to them.—Mary Moran and Henry Salt did not appear to answer a similar summons, and warrants were issued for their apprehension.

A BURDEN TO RUNCORN RATEPAYERS.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, James Millington, a rough- looking fellow, was charged that he being a person able to work and maintain himself and family did neglect to do so. whereby his wife and children had become charge- , able to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. W. H. Linaker, deputy clerk to the Guardians, prosecuted.— Mr. G.. Ward, the relieving officer, said the prisoner's wife and six children had been inmates of Dutton Work- house for three years, and they had cost the 'Union the sum of zB3 17s. One of the children had recently died. —Mr. Garratt, foreman to Messrs. T. Kirkham and Co., said the prisoner could have regular work if he would .attend to it. In August several gentlemen interes. ted themselves in the prisoner;" and Mr. Kirkjiam instructed witness to start him at 48. per day. The prisoner worked from the Thursday until the Monday, and be then went on the "spree."—The prisoner was sentenced, to a month's hard labour. .

POACHING AT RnNcon.x.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, a young man named Thomas Lydiate, whose home is in Bridgewater-street, was charged with poaching on land in the occupation of Mr. John Ackerley, fanner, Halton. The prisoner pleaded guilty.—lt appeared that about nine o'clock on the night of Wednesday, the sth inst., the prisoner and several other men were observed along- side Haddocks Wood at Astmoor. George Rigby, game- keeper to Sir Richard Brooke, went towards them, but with the exception of the prisoner the men escaped. The prisoner struck Rigby a blow on the face with a heavy coat he had in his hand, but he was overpowered and arrested. In his pockets twelve large stones, and also a rabbit were found, and on the ground two nets, a num- ber of pegs, and several coats were lying.—The prisoner said he had never been out poaching before. He was drunk at the time or he should not have gone.—The keeper said he was much troubled with poachers at Ast- moor, and the Bench lined the prisoner £2 and costs, 15s. fkt.,. or in default a month's hard labour. The money was paid. THE RETIREMENT OF COLONEL THACHWELL. The "London Gazette" of Tuesday last contained the retirement of Colonel Thackwell, C. 8., from the command of the Bth regimental district, with the ' honorary rank of major-general. It is understood that Colonel Thackwell has promised to becmie the honorary colonel of the 15th L.R.V. It is rumoured in volunteer circles that the commanding officer of the 15th did not take his officers into his confidence with regard to this step, but merely announced it after it was settled, and after they had heard all about it from outsiders. It is also stated that the officers feel very sore at what they consider a and that it will not tend to improve the relationship between their C. 0. and themselves.—Lirerposi Mer- cury.

VISCOUNT CEOSS ON THE limn QUESTION Viscount Cross, addressing a meeting of the Northern Union Cbnservative Association at Carlisle on Thursday afternoon, urged that, on the question of Ireland. they must Tay aside party feeling, and they would find the great majority of the people of England and Scotland would be on their side. He welcomed the co-operation of both Liberals and Radicals. He thought the loyal people of Ireland had hitherto been discouraged through fear that the Imperial Government would ignore them. They might dismiss the idea absolutely, and be certain that as long as the present Government 6xlsted they would stand by those loyal men, and take care they were not interfered with by agitators, whereever they came from. He was quite sure if they freed the people of Ireland from the thraldom and tyranny towhich they had been subjected they would not vote as hitherto. _

MARRIAGE Or SIR A. B. WALXF.R. On Tues- day, the marriage of Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, Baronet, of Gateacre Orange, and Osmaston Manor, Derbyshire, to, the 'Honourable Maude Okeover, second daughter of Mr. IfOughton Charles Okeover, of Okeover-Hall, Staffordshire, was celebrated in the private chapel at Okeover Ball. The ceremony was arranged to take place early in the summer, but owing to the illness of Sir Andrew it had to be postponed, who, after a short sojourn in Scotland, again recovered his wonted state of health. There are few men in this part of the country who are more widely known or more highly respected than Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, whose acts of beneficence and generosity have made his name a household word. The bride is a member of one of the oldest families in the kingdom, Okeover having been the seat of her ancestors since the time of the Conquest. She is a young lady of high at- tainments, and has mingled with the highest class of society. Her Majesty the Queen was amongst the numerous persons who presented gifts to the bride,

THR PRRSCOT WATCHMAKING INDUSTRY. On Tuesday a meeting was held in the Prescot Town Hall to consider the proposal to establish a factory in Prescot for the complete manufacture of watches. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Harry Mitchell, vicar of Prescot, who alluded to the distress in Pres- cot, and said he had called the, meeting to see.if the process of drifting in the trade of Prescot could not be arrested. The majority of the people had a de- cided preference for English-made watches, the re- tail price of which was 100 per cent. more than the cost price, while the Amerman watches sold at an average profit of 2s 6d. Present supplied the Eng- lish trade with the highest class movements at the lowest margin of profits while the London and Coventry makers took the harvest.--Mr. F. P. Hewitt, watch manufacturer (representative of the Prescot Watchmakers' Association at the Royal Commis- sion}. said the reason for the non-success in watch- making was they were trib-divided ; they made for so many little makers that they were not in a posi- tion to put down the machinery and tools necessary to produce movementS of the very cheapest kind. The public wanted them to inake the best watches possible cheaply. The Americans were doing this and leaving us in the cold.—Further discussion fol- lowed, and a resolution was carried unanimously that it was desirable to establish in Prescqt a fac- tory for the manufacture of efficient vratebes as cheaply as possible.

ALLEGED FRAUD BY A WIDNES ENGINEICR. Mr. H. Wade-Deacon was engaged a considerable time at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, investi- gating a charge against David Proctor Jones, engi- neer and fitter, Birchfield-lane, Parnworth. The accusation was that he had knowingly, arid with intent to defraud, obtained by false pretences the sum of LI from William Leatherbarrow, contractor at the Widnes Alkali Works. Mr. Shand, barrister (in- structed by Mr. T. J. Peters), appeared to prosecute, and the defence was undertaken by Mr. Mulholland, barrister (instructed by Mr. Percy Davies, of Warring- , ton.) From the statement of Mr. Shand and the evi- dence adduced, it .apneared that on various occasions Leatherbarrow had advanced sums ofmoney to Jones for specific purposes in connection with his business. At the end of last year Jones was in want of a lathe, and in December Leatherbarrow- advanced money to buy a lathe and a further sum of £7 to pay for the removal of the machine to Parnworth. In that month it was discovered during a valuation of the stock on the • premises occupied by Jones that the lathe was not of the value stated, and inquiries revealed tho fact that Jones had paiduved the 'machine for £lO.

-I Hence these proceedings. During the cross ex- amination of Leatherbarrow it transpired that ' the premises occupied by Jones are the property of the former, and that he had taken possession of them, together with all machinery, books, and papers. In consequence Jones commenced an action against Leather- barrow, on the Bth September, for breaking into and entering the premises and for the return of all the chat- ties, &c., contained therein. The sum of £450 was claimed as damages for the detention of the machinery, &c., and the case is set down for hearing at Liverpool Assizes. In his statement of defence Leatherbarrow claimed the identical £7 for which he now brought criminal proceedings, and his solicitor had suggested an amicable settlement of all the matters in dispute.—After hearing several witnesses 4 Mr. Deacon thought there was a prima facie case, and committed the defendant to the Quarter qessions for trial. Bail of two sureties at £4O each was accepted.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. E. Carey took the chair, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. Sadler, .1. Houghton, H. Gaskell, jun., F. Heyes, D. Wright. B. Cook, J. Midwood, B. Brown, W. W. Gossage, and T. Handley; J. T. Allln (clerk), W. Higginson (sur- veyor), J. Dickson (nuisance inspector). AUDITOR'S REPORT: WHISKEY AND BRANDY AT ELECTIONS.

Mr. George Hazlehurst, district auditor, reported that he had completed the audit of the accounts of the Board I for the year ended at Lady Day last, and he was pleased to state that he found the same during the past year had been kept in a generally correct and satisfactory man- ner. There was, however, in his opinion, room forim- provement in the mode of keeping the gas and water stores account, and he should like to see a sys. tern in force by which a more adequate check cauld be placed on these stores. He felt it his duty to disallow several payments in their account in connection with the gas exhibition held last rear under the auspices of the Board, there being, in his opinion, no lawful authority for such expenditure. During the past year the Board had expended upon the Public Free Library building £248 as. 9d. in excess of the amount of the loan sapctioned by the Local Government "Board, and as he considered it open to grave dqubt whether such excess could properly be considered Ns forming part of their ex- penditure on the public offices loan account. He would strongly stnnmend the Board to apply for further bor- rowing powers on free library account in order to enable them to take up loans sufficient to cover the entire cost of the Free Library building.—The Clerk said the Audi- tor in the usual course had before him the amounts of expenses at the Local Board election for 1889, and across on bill he had written a note which he desired him (Mr. Allen) to bring before the Board. The note read as 'fol- lows :—" I think the charges for whiskey and brandy excessive—(laughter)—to say nothing of excessive quan- tities consumed, and hope to see considerable reduction on any future occasion."—Mr. Onok : Put Mr. Brown on. (Laughter.)—The Clerk observed that Mr. Grossage, who was the returning offieer at the time, asked that the ex- pense should not be so great in future.—Dr. O'Keeffe drew attention to the fact that there was no need for whiskey or wine at the last election.—The auditors re- port was referred to the Finance Committee. The bill referred to was from Mr. Chapman, of the Grosvenor Hotel, and contained the follqwing items :-29 dinners and teas, £4 Ts. ; two bottles bf brandy, 145. ; three bot- tles of whiskey, 155.; five bottles ofclaret, £1 55.; one bottle of port wine, 55.; mineral waters, 125.; bitter beer, Ts. ; cigars, £1 15s. ; total, £lO.

div.head: CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.
div.p: CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.

Mr. James Rimmer, of 51, Victoria-road, wrote that on Tuesday, the 4th inst., he was driving along Melton- road, when suddenly his horse fell and cut his knees badly. The shafts, trap, and harness were also broken. He found that the accident occurred through the „road being in a bad state, and he trusted the Board would make him some recompense for the damage done. He enclosed a bill for £l4, including £lO for damage to horse.—The letter was referred to the Highway Com- mittee.
CLAIM FOR LOSS BY SEWER CONSTRUCTION.

Martin Rossiter, of 22, Lugsdale-road, claimed com- pensation for the blocking of his shop door during the construction of the sewer, which caused milk and vege- tables to be thrown on his hands.--Refened to the com- mittee.

div.head: MR. HVSBAND RESIGNS.
div.p: MR. HVSBAND RESIGNS.

Mr. W. T. Itusba-n.d-,-th-e-iie-pt7;C:o-rOner, wrote to the chairman as follows :=" Finding that I cannot devote that attention to Local Board work that membership entails, I beg to tender my resignation, in the hope that your Board may find someone to fill the vacancy better able to attend the meetings than I have been."—ln reply to some observations, Mr. Gaskelftaid Mr. Husband had spoken some time ago of taking this step, and'he was i very decided about t. He moved that the resignation be accepted, and that Mr. Husband be thanked for his services.—Mr. Cook seconded the proposition,which was carried unanimously.
THE WATER SUPPLY.-ASSESSMENT OF GAS AND WATER WORKS.

The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee con- tained an analysis of samples of water from Stockswelf and Netherley by Dr. Campbell Brown, who remarked as follows :—" both samples are very pure and clean. A microscopic examination shows nothing but what is found in the best waters, and is in fact almost negat- tive, although Ido observe, on standing, a small num- ber of living organisms at the bottom of the bottle. These are microscopic in size, and of the lowest orders, and develope in most waters on standing." According to instructions given, Mr. Newbigging, of Manchester, had made a valuation of the gas and water, with the following result :—Waterworks, £5,818 ; gas works, £1,844. Mr. Allen, the clerk, had previously made a vahration, showing waterworks £5,552, gas works £1,728. In 1885 the assessment of the water- works was £5,360, was raised to £7,698 in 1886, and was subsequently reduced to £8,742. The assessment of the gas works in 1885 was £3,102, was raised to £3,103 m 1888, and was subsequently reduced to £2,505.—1t was recommended that the contract with Mr. Newbigging for valuing (1 per cent on the net rate- able value and travelling expenses) be sealed. It was further recommended that Messrs. Oppenheim and Malkin be instructed to appeal against the assessments at the Quarter Q,cgsions.—Adopted.
HIGHWAY MATTERS.

The minutes of the Highway Committee contained a letter from Mr. J. R. Wylde, asking who is responsible foralleged neglect at sewerage works, Victoria-road. In- structions given to reply that the contractor is respon- sible for excavations in such work. Letter from Mrs Ashley, claiming compensation for damage to horse and trap, owing to sewerage works, Victoria-road. The Clerk reported that the claim had been settled by con- tractor.—Main Sewers : Letter, 28th September, from the Widnes Alkali Co., asking if the proposed sewer through Widnes Marsh will provide for the acid drainage from the Tharsis Co's. works. Instructions given to reply that the Tharsis works will not be connected to the pro- posed sewer.—The minutes were adopted on the propo- sition of Mr. Carey.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The Medical Officer reported to the committee that during September there were 97 births and 59 deaths, being at the rate, respectively, of 381' and 23-6 per 1,000. There werel6 deaths amongst children under orve year and 16 amongst children between one and five years. Zymotic disease caused 21 deaths. The Medical Officer added that he was sorry to have to report that several cases of typhoid fever had occurred during the month, and he earnestly impressed on the Board the ad- visability of furnishing the Infectious Di:eases Hospital as soon as possible.—The committee recommended that a matron be advertised for at asalary of Eso per annum: that a servant be engaged, and that assistant nurses be engaged as required. It was also recommended that £2OO be provided in the estimate for the furnishing of the hos- pital and house.—Dr. O'Keeffe moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Gaskell said there would not be an im- provement in the general health of the town until there was an alteration in the system of nightsoil removal, and the work was effectually carried out. Dr. Page, of the Local Government Board, only twelve months ago had urged that the work of nightsoil removal should be undertaken by the Board.—Mr. Brown asked whether there were not powers given to the Board in the con- tract, to carry out work neglected by the contractor at the contractor's cost.—Dr. O'Keeffe said there had been a great many complaints made from time to time against the contractor, and he had in consequence been repri- manded and fined very heavily. On numerous occasions other persons had been engaged to remove the nightsoil at the contractor's expense. At present the committee were endeavouring to adopt a better method. but they did not think it worth while to take the contract away when it was so near terminating. No doubt the pro- longed drought and the high temperature was the cause of the heavy death rate in August, of 37 per I,ooo.—Mr. Gaskell thought the contractor had grossly neglected his business' and that this fact had contributed to the high death rate. He considered the Commissioners would be quite justified in putting an end to the contract at once.—Dr. O'Keeffe said if the Board came to that de- cision the committee 'would carry it out.—The minutes were adopted.

NEW ELATE. The Finance Committee submitted the following esti- mates 2—Expenditure for half-year ending September, 1887, £5,638; Highway Committee's estimate for half- year ending March, 1888, £2,331; Health Committee's ditto, £1,076; Finance Committee's ditto, £2,504 ; total, £11,549. Less balance of income and expenditure ac- count at end of March, /887, £1,355; collections and arrears for half-year ending September, 1887, £5,098. Nett requirements, £&O9B.—Recommended that a rate •of is. in the £ be laid for the half-year ending March, 1888 estimated to produce £5,096. The minutes were approved on• the motion of Mr. Handley, and tlw• meeting terminated.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY NIGHT. It is a fact, the significance of which the person principally concerned is too shrewd not to observe, that Mr. Chamberlain's visit to Ireland excites sin- gularly little attention. Able editors, accustomed to-guage public interest in a current question, are agreed that a comparatively brief summary of what Mr. Chamberlain says to the loyal men of Ulster will meet the public demand. For the first time for the last seven years, Mr. Chamberlain, embarked upon a political campaign, is not reported in the first person in the London newspapers. He knows what that means, and may, perhaps, profit by the information. Mr. Chamberlain, able man though hq be, is at the present moment of no particular consel quence because he has cordmitted himself tea hope- less enterprise. He made a mistake the consequence of which will certainly follow him through all his political life, and he is now with characteristic stubbornness and obstinacy following it up. He is' the Mrs Partington of our politics of to-day, trying to brush back the steadily rising tide of the Atlan- tic of public opinion that will presently bring in Home Rule for Ireland. There is something par- ticularly comical in the notion of Mr. Chamberlain. a man of the people accustomed to appeal to the people, betaking himself to a small and well-defined minority of the population and addressing. them as if they were the people. it is, remembering past days, a pitiful exhibition, and the sooner Mr. Cham- berlain gets away on his well advised visit to the United States the better for him. Perhaps the most striking thing in his Ulster speeches, as far as they have gone, is the develop- ment of his position of personal antipathy, and would-be rivalry to Mr. Gladstone. Hitherto he has succeeded in preserving a certain mask of friendli- ness. He has sat on a fence prepared to drop down on whichever side might offer the greater advan- tage. Up to the last skirmish in the House of Com- mons, Mr. Gladstone was still "my right hon. friend," and so, though with a preceptible snort, was Mr. John Morley. Now Mr. Chamberlain girds at Mr Gladstone in the fine old manner of a Conserva- tive hack speaker, whilst his wrath . grows incon- trollable when he is obliged to refer to Mr. Morley. He has at last taken up his proper place, which is something gained. It has been an embarrassing position in view of his attitude for everyone actively engaged in politics. Among the rank and file of the party, those masses to whom he used so confidently to appeal, there has been for at least a year a downright hearty disgust with his tactics. They have hooted his name when it has been men- tioned from the platform, and have been anxious above all things to see him drummed out of the party. With the circle that more closely surrounds Mr. Gladstone, there has been a desire to leave a door open for the rebel when the time came that he found rebellion was not a paying game. This feel- ing found issue in the Round Table Conference. It was not destroyed, though it received a severe check, when one fine day Mr. Chamberlain left the Round Table glowing with newly-revived friend- ship to write his famous letter to the "Baptist." It was always thought that he might come back, and if he did he should not be rudely rtpulsed. But now that increasingly uncomfortable condition of affairs is ever. He has gone over bag and baggage to the enemy, and from the safe bastions of Belfast shakes a puny fist ill tbe face of Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party. The whole business is a miserable one, inasmuch as it had its birth entirely with personal considera- tions. If Mr. Disraeli had been in Mr. Gladstone's place eighteen months ago, Mr. Chamberlain would never havelound himself in the strange company he now keeps. Mr. Gladstone, whilst acknowledg- ing Mr. Chamberlain's conspicuous ability, wag , never personally drawn to him as he was to Lord ' Hartington, and is now to Mr. Morley. With all his gemus, be is notoriously lacking in *t in his dealings with those who work w' him for the common cause. He is neve- careful not to ruffie personal sensibilit,ie- .4 as Mr. Disraeli always was. It ....manion-plade observation among Mr. Chamber- -4aln's old friends and colleagues. that if the mem- ber for Birmingham had been made a Secretary of State, we should never have heard of the Liberal Unionists, still less of the National party, which for ' the present seems to be hiding its head in obscurity. But Mr. Gladstone did not otter Mr. Chamberlain a a Secretaryship of State, and, worse still, he took Mr. John Morley and made him Chief Secretary for Ireland, with a seat in the Cabinet, actually on a footingeof equality with Mr. Chamberlain, who had , looked forward to a period when he might make ' use of the member for Newcastle as a kind of first- class Jesse Collings. Doubtless the story of Mr. Chamberlain's defection will some day be told in detail and with authority. It will be a page of history not calculated to imbue the mind of the student with a high view of imperial politics. Meanwhile, the main facts are already sufficiently well known to throw a clear light on the excursions to Ulster and elsewhere of a politician who is above all a Radical with a wholesome contempt for those "who toil not, neither do they spin." Passing by the Mansion House this morning, I saw an elderly gentleman facing with remarkable I presence of mind the dangers of the maelstrom that eddies there. Of all the dangerous crossings in Lon- don, there is nothing like that by the Mansion House, where seven or eight great thoroughfares meet, and the tide of pedestrians and vehicular traffic surges all day. The old gentleman made his way through the throng as coolly as if he were an agile youth, and safely landed on the distant pavement. It was a familiar figure in the House of Commons, and had he attempted to cross the much more acces- sible thoroughfare at the bottom of Parliament- street, half a dozen policemen would have rushed to stop the traffic. It was none other than Mr. C. P. Villiers—pronounce " Villars," after the arbitrary fashion in dealing with proper names. Mr. Villiers was born in the second year of the century, and has reached an age when it is wonderful to find him about, much less crossing over by the Mansion House. Mr. Christopher Talbot, member for Gla- morganshire, is father of the House of Commons, entering five years earlier than Mr. Villiers began his uninterrupted representation of Wolverhampton. But of the two Mr. Villiers is the older man, and whilst Mr. Talbot is rarely seen in London, Mr. Vil- liers is constant in his attendance at the House of Commons, and fearlessly faces the dangers of the London streets. He does not now take any part in debate, and it is almost forgotten that once upon a time he was President of the Poor Law Board for fully seven years. Another old member of the House of Commons is, lam sorry to say, not in the enjoyment of such robust health. Mr. Beresford Hope is quite a chicken compared to Mr. Villiers, being only in his sixty-seventh year. But he has been a broken man since the death of his wife six years ago. Up to that date he was a constant attendant upon his Par- liamentary duties, and a frequent speaker. His "Bata.vian Grace" has been made familiar in the ears of the public by a memorable phrase of his old adversary, Mr. Disraeli. He had possessed himself of the corner seat below the gangway, whence, holding on to himself with both hands tugging at his coat collar,he delivered manyamusing speeches, of which he himself was invariably the most de- lighted auditor. But he fell upon evil times. The Fourth Party, led by Lord Randolph Churchill, gra- dually elbowed him out of the seat he had held for a generation. They finally succeeded in evicting him, and after some timid efforts to get himself taken back as caretaker, Mr. Beresford Hope crossed the gangway, and availing himself of his right as a Privy Councillor, took his seat on the Front Bich. Ido not remember to have seen him once last session, and fear we may not see him in any succeeding session. A private letter from Mr. Robert Louis Stevenson gives an encouraging account of "Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde," who have come out in fresh quarters.
TW WRONG SIDE UP. • EY EDWIN WAUGH. (From "Black and White.") "Now, hasto bin wi' the witches Fth cloof, at deep o'th fleet? Come, tell me, Robin, tell me, For some'at is not reet !"
- .31Y Son Robin. "I can make nonther top nor tail o' this!' Old Saying.

It was a keen December day, and the trees of the vicarage were festooned with benutiful frost-work. Crisp snow lay thick upon the old church, and upon the tombs and gravestones of the churchyard, and upon the roofs of the houses around; but upon the street where the cattle market had been held, it

was now trampled into slush, and soiled by the business of the day. The crowd was thinning, for evening was creeping on, and folk had begun to " tak the gate." Cattle, sold and unsold, were slowly wending away from the scene, with their drivers at their heels; and the quaint old street, where the market had been held for centuries, was gradually sinking down to its usual stillness. But as the light of day declined, the glow of the kitchen fire grew stronger in the Royal Oak, a famous old hostelry in front of the churchyard, where Bill Holland and Ben Boswell, two comfort- able butchers, had crept into the chimney corner for a quiet chat and a glass, before retiring for the night to their old haunts in the middle of the town. "Between thee an' me, Ben," said Bill Holland, "bar-foot folk should'nt walk upo' prickles." "Well, one would think so," replied Ben, "but it just depends whether they liken it or not, thou knows." _

"Well,—ay,—as thou says Ben. If they liken to torment theirsels, they're welcome to fill their bellies, as far as I'm consarzet—as long as they keepen it to theirsels, and don't trouble other folk. But, between thee an' me. I tell tho again, there's a lot o' craiters i' this world that are never comfortable. Sich folk should be kept in a bit of a pinfowd by theirsels," "They're awk'ard crater& to live wi', for sure. But what ails him? They sey'n he's as rich as Cheetham o' Castleton." _ .

"Rich! What's th' use o' that, if a chap's thrutched in his mind? Folks cannot height (eat) gowd ! When brass gets pile't up to that pitch, it bides a deal o' tentin' and lookin' after. Now, th' difference between five thousan' an' five million pounds is o' book-keepin' an anxiety. I consider that a mon's no more goods i' this world than what he can get good out on. If he'd o' th' brass i' Eng-, lan' he could nobbut sleep i' one bed at a time; and if his brass troubles his mind, he'd better b poor." "I don't like being poor mysel', Bill. But there's someat i' what thou says,: for o' that. If a chap's o'enveighted in his mind he's in an ill case,--an it doesn't matter whether it's slutch or gowd,-- if it poos him down." "It's a feaw life havin' too much brass, Den.' "Well, I never tried it." "Nawe, nor me noather. That's a boggart that never freeten't noather thee nor me, Ben. . . .

But, come,—here's a Merry Christmas, owd lad!" 1 " Th' same to thee, Bill! It'll be here, now, in a week or two—as who lives to see it. . . . But, I yer there's one or two on em down i'th' town that's started their Christmas rather afore th' time."

"Oh, ay! Who's.that ?" "Well, owd Cushy, an' Nukkin, an' Bob Leech, an' Occy Lee, an' one or two mobre. They'n bin agate o their marlocks down rth owd street, yon, I yer. It wur Occy Lee that towd me about it." •Ay what wur it ?" "Well, it seems that some on 'em turned th' Gow- _ _.

den Bo' sign th' wrong side up toner fleet." "Oh, ay! An' it's true enough, ebo ! It wur Bob Leech that did it i'th neat-time. Tother knew nougt about it. . . But, didto yer what a prank Nukkin an'owei Vastly had wi this sign th' next In.91104'?" a Not a "Well, UM kebws, Nukkin an owd Cushy are two tith driest-throated craiters there is 1' this country; an they're generally up- afore onybody else in a mornin' huntin' for some at to sup. ; th' mornin' after, owd Bob bad turn't this sign wrong side up, these two coon/ trailin' down th' street together, soon after break o' day, eerattin' their yeds, an' tootin' about for th' first alehouse dur that oppen't ! an' when they geet to th' front o'th Gowden Bo', Cushy looked up at th' sign, an' , he said, ' Hello ! what's owd Dan Nield bin doin' wi' his sign?' This is noan o' Dan's ! ' said Nukkitt, l'Yigh, it is!,, said Cushy. Yigh, it is! I know by I th' windows!' It's noan o'th same sign, then,' said Nukkin. 'I cannot read it.' Well, Cushy seed that th' sign wur wrong side up, so he said, ' Come to tother side o'th road, here; an' ston on thi yed up , agen th' wall; an' then thou'll read it fast enough! Well," said Nukkin, Ifeel raither tickle-stomacked this mornin', when I•na th' reet end up; but have a try at this jeb !' An' down went his yed; an up went his legs again th' wall. Now. Cushy,' said Nukteuf, thou mun keep howd on me, or else I'se tvlver be able to stick up; for I'm noblint wambly when I'm stonin' o' mi feet!' Here, I'll steady tho a bit, owd lad.' said Cushy. An' he went an' kept, his feet up again th' wall. Now, then, said Cushy, conto make it out?' 'Make it out? Nawe, by 'th' mass,' said Nukkin, • It's ten times worse than it wur when I stood o' mi feet! Th' whole house is th' wrong side up, now !"Conto read th' name upo' th' sign?' Nawe,' said Nukkin. I can mak noather top nor tail on't ! I'm not one o'th best readers i'th world when I'm th' reet end up; but there isn't a worse scholar alive than me—when I'm stonnin' on mi yed! . . . Nay, it's no use! I connot make it out! Let me come down ! " Thou hasn't gin it a fair chance yet, mon, said Cushy. 'Thou'll manage it with a bit more practice. Try it again, while thou art there!" ' Here, thee let go my legs,' said Nukkin, 'an come an' have a try thi- I would, in a minute,' said Cushy, but I've a sore place on th' top o' my yed.' 'Ay,' said Nukkin; an' I's have a sore place o' my yed, too, if I stop here much longer! Let go my legs, I tell tho I 'Just have another whet at it,' said Cushy, ' an' then I'll let tho comedown! . . . • Conto make aught on it now ? ' 'Not a bit,' said Nukkin. 'lt's like a whisketful o' chips! An' as for th' letters, they're o' masht up together, like a ponful o' lobscouse There is one letter amung 'em; an' that's an 0— that's o' I can mak Out! Let go my legs, I tell tho— an' let me come down—l'm gettin' as mazy as a tup ! It's noan o'th same house!' So Cushy lest go his legs, an' down he eoom like a seek o' potitos ; an' he had to lie theere awhile afore he could gether his wits together again." "It's just like 'em. . . . But, come; I mun be off down into th' town. . . I guess thou'll be lookin' in at th' Blue Bell some time afore th' fleet's o'er?" "I'll meet tho at th' 'Amen Corner,' if thou's a mind, at nine o'clock ! " "Agreed on!"

The Exchange Telegraph Company learns that there is no alteration in the low condition of Madame Goldsmidt (Jenny Lind). Her friend§ have no hopes of her re- covery. The barque Jules came off the bar at Padstow on Mon- day evening, but capsized and sank in the Channel. One boy was drowned, and the cargo was on Tuesday Boat- ing about in the harbour. The death is announced of Lady Brassey. Her lady- ship, who was returning from Australia on board the Sunbeam, was seized with fever, and died on the 14th ult. See was buried at sea. The Beevor Hall Works, near Barnsley, where Messrs. Wilson & Co. carried on an extensive business as bobbin manufacturers, were partially destroyed by fire early on Thursday morning. The St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway is the name of a new line which has just been announced. The prospectus will be found in another column, and we think it will be clear, after a perusal of this document and a glance at the accompanying map, that the scheme presents more than ordinary attractions to the investor. We are led to make this observation from various reasons, which do not apply to the ordinary prospectuses of railway companies. Taking the document in ifs own order, it will be seen that the board of directors consists of gentlemen of the highest repute and standing—such men, in fact, as, without reflecting utxm any other com- pany, used in the good old days of genuine railway en- terprise to undertake the management of new under- takings. The member of Parliament for the borough of St. Helens heads the list as chairman. The deputy chair,. man is a member of one of the most progressive and suc- cessful firms in the chemical trade in St. Helens, and the remaining directors are the Right Hon. Lord Gerard and William John Legh, Esq., of Lyme Park, D.L.,a former representative of South Lancashire in Parliament, and which two gentlemen are together the most important landowners on the line of route. div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday roust be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later titan ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUOBY RULES. HOWLEY ROVERS V. Jocanic STAR. Played on the ground of the Rovers, on Saturday. A stubborn game ensued, resulting as follows :—Rovers, 2 tries, 7 minors to nil.
WARRINGTON ST:ALBANS 2ND v. PLATT BRIDGB 2ND.—. Played on the ground of the former, and resulted in a drowhi favcw Of the visitors by 2 minors to St. Albans 1 minor.
HALTON v. FRODSHAM 2ND.—This match was played at Halton on Saturday, and after a splendid game resulted in a win for the home team by 2 tries, 2 disputed tries, 7 minors to nil.

SANKEY v. 'WARRINGTON 2ND.—This match was played on Saturday. Sankey had the best of the game through- out, and eventually won by one try, four minors, to Warrington one minor. RUNCORN (2ND TRAM) v. NEW BRIGHTON OLTMPIC. Played at Liscard on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by one goal, two tries, and five minor points to the Olympic nil. The home team played four men short, only two "twenties" being played. The tries were obtained by F. Hancock, J. Gratley, and E. Lunt.

RITNCORIV OLD BOYS v. LITCHFORD.—This match was played at Latchford. Good football was out of the question in consequence of the slippery state of the ground. In the first half Boden ran half the length of the field, and scored a splendid try for the visitors. In the second half nothing but minors were scored. Result :—Old Boys, one try, three minors; Latchford, nil.

ST. PAUL'S (2ND) v. LOWBR HOUSE TRI7B BLOBS.-St. Paul's journeyed on Saturday to St. Helens to play their fixture with the above club with only eleven men, but they had able substitutes found by the home team. When no side was:tvliiiitled the game was won by St. Paul's, they having scored 1 try and 9 minors to nll. For the visitors Sudlow and Scott, three-quarters' and Evans, half back, were the pick of the backs, whilst the for- wards one and all worked hard. _

GRANGE, BIRKENHEAD, V. FRODSHAM IST.—This match was played on the ground of the latter, and owing to the bad state of the weather two 20 minutes were de- cided upon. Frodsham proved the victors by two tries and five minors to one minor. Teams e' Full back, A. Ball; three-quarter backs, T, jories, C. Wool- ridge, and T. Hughes; half backs, J. Roberts and Dry- deli; forwards, &mut, Henderson, Moore, At- kinson Fogg, Griffiths, .E. , C. Hughes. Frodsham Ist: back, Goodall ; three-quarter backs, G. Webb, J. Mercer, f. Darlington, T. Rogers; half backs, J. Ashworth, W. Tudor; forwards' W. Dimelow, J. Fletcher, f's Thomas, S. Helsby, J. Garner, W. Miller, Briscoe, and W. H. Heyes. WYCLIFFE RANGERS V. WYCLIFFB (2ND).—Thi5 Ittateh was played on Saturday on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a victory for the Rangers by one goal, eight minors, to nil. The weather was very unpropitious, rain falling heavily during the whole of the game. Wycliffe won the toss, and elected to play with the wind. The first half of the game was very evenly con- tested, one minor only being scored by the Rangers. In the second half the visitors had nearly all their own way, keeping the ball continually in their opponents' 25, minor succeeding minor in quick succession. In the last five minutes the Rangers, by a good rush, took the ball over the line, Potter securing a try, from which Weir kicked a nice goal, just before the call of time. Roughley, as three-quarter, and Miller in the forwards, played a good game for the winners, and J. Ball at three-quarter, and Samson at full back were the pick of the Wycliffe team. WIDNES v. MOSSLEY.—These teams met at Widnes on Saturday in miserable weather, notwithstanding which at least 2,000 people lined the enclosure. Rain fell heavily during the whole of the game, and thus pre- vented any exhibition of scientific play. The game was very well contested, the teams being evenly matched, but the result was a victory for the visitors by a goal, a try, and 3 minors, to 6 minors. This was a result scarcely expected by anybody, still less by the Widnesians. Teams :—Widnes: S. Bingham, back; Morris, Parkinson, and Plumpton, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Wilkin- son, half-backs; Smith (captain), Kiddie, Hardman, J. Bingham, Woods, Fogg, Gandy, Barber, and H. Hughes, forwards. Mossley : Marsden, back ; Joe Winterbottom, Wood, and Niel, three-quarter backs; Billings and Booth, half-backs; Mayan (captain), Firth, Newby, Rowen, Mitchell, Walker, Hobson, Coxe, and James Winterbot- tOM, forwards. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER FREE WANDERERS ("A" Talms).—This match was played at Fallowfield on Sat- urday in a heavy downpour of rain, which prevented the Warrington backs from displaying their passing qualities to anything like the same advantage they did the week previous at Walton; but the forwards played a grand game, and at times completely outplayed their opponents, who were a heavy lot. The home captain won the toss, and Whittle kicked off against the wind and rain at 3-45, play resting in centre. Whittle passed to Evans, who kicked into touch in the Wanderers' quarters. The Warrington forwards dribbled to the home full back, who secured and kicked to Daniels, this player in running the ball back being brought down by Smith. The Free Wanderers' forwards broke away with the ball, but Randalls stopped their progress by sending the oval into touch in the Warrington 25. Evans got in a good kick and, following up, prevented a return being made. From a scrimmage in the centre of the field the ball was kicked by Antrobus to Evans, who made a short run and then passed to Daniels, the latter player running to near' the line, where he passl to Nevins. Nevins in turn transferred to Randalls, wholad no diffi- culty in getting. over. Isherwood vms unsuccessful at the place. Bailey kicked off, and after two or three scrimmages near midfield Walsh, Thornley, and Eyes I dribbled the ball over the line, Holt touching down. The home captain dropped out, but the ball was brought back for offside play. McCall now got possession of the ball and put in a splendid run and kick to the Warring- ton quarter flag, Jolley sending the ball into touch. The visiting forwards took play to centre, where Evans picked up nicely, and, running strongly, passed all but the full back, when he passed to Daniels, this player grounding the ball between the posts, Isherwood kicking a goal from an easy position. Bailey restarted, , and'the visiting forwards dribbled the leather tp Holt, ' who made a grand run, but Evans tackled him, and kicked into touch. Jones, Hackett, Randalls' and Whittle were instrumental in taking play to theWan- derers' quarters, McCall relieving the pressure by kick- ing into touch. Antrobus saved a rush of the home for- wards, but .Anderton again came away with the ball;

Jolley neutralized by kicking into touch near the home quarter flag. Thornley broke away from the line out, but McCall secured and put in a short run, being brought down by Nevins. Molyneaux, Jones, and Walsh dribbled to the line, but Hulme relieved by a timely kick, and Boardman failing to return play rested in Warrington territory. Holt here passed to McCall, who was held by Boardman. Hackett, Thotnley, and Nevins headed a dribble to centre, and Antrobus passed to Evans, who took a drop at goal, a Minor resulting. Half time being called, the score stood—Warrington one goal, one try, and two minor points, to Free Wanderers nil. During the second half Warrington kept the upper hand, and won by two goals, three ties, and seven minor points, to Manchester Free Wanderers nil. Teams Warrington: Full back, Jolley; threequarter backs, Boardman, Evans, and Daniels; half backs, Whittle (captain), and Antrobus ; forwards, Molyneaux, I Thornley, Hackett, Eyes, Nevins, Jones, Walsh Ran- dant, and Isherwood. Free Wanderers: Full back. F. Hole • threequarter backs, Hulme, McCall, and Smith; half backs E. C. Holt and E. Nickson ; forwards, E. Bailey (captain), Oswald, H. H. Anderton, Owen, Dain, Thorpe, Janson, Knight, and Bettney.

div.head: RUNCORN V. NEW BRIGHTON.
div.p: RUNCORN V. NEW BRIGHTON.

This match was decided at Runcorn on Saturday, in wet weather, before a moderate attendance, rain des- cending heavily during the seventy minutes the players were on the field, thus rendering the going heavy and good passing at a discount, though in this respect the home team shone particularly well considering the greasy condition of the ball. Runcorn were without W. Hughes and Wainwright, whilst R. Barber was the most conspicuous absentee on the visiting side. The latter played a new three-quarter in the perm of Her- bert Dodd, who, judging from the chances he had—and few they were—of distinguishing himself, is likely to prove an acquisition to the New Brighton club, his clever tackling being much admired. Runcorn won the toss, New Brighton kicking off. The game culminated in the home team w inningby three goals, three tries and five minor points to 1 minor. Mr. F. T. Parry acted as referee. Players: Runcorn: T. -Woods, back; T. Davies H. C. Speakman, and H. Cawley, three-quarter backs'; H. Hughes (captain) and H. G. Andrews, half-backs; Wright W. Clarke, J. Lew', W. Faulkner, T. Riley, J. nartig, w. Broatly, E. Andrews, and J. Hotana, forwards. New Brighton: C. J. Luya, bac nerbert Dodd, R. Woodward, and W. Male, three-quarter k backs; Q. J. Leitch and C. Woodward, half-backs; Harry Dodd, W. Dutton, S. It Williams, J.H. Williams, IJ. W. Patton, L. W. Jones, F. Toppin, Gifford, and F. W. Jones (captain) forwards.

WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER FREE WANDERERS. This match Was played at Warrington on Saturday last. The weather was very unfavourable, and conse- quently Affected the attendance, but notwithstanding this drawback, there would be close on 1,500 spectators aseembled to witness the encounter. The visitors were without the services of Bull and Cockerill, whilst from the ranks of the home team Fair Turner and Littlewood were absent. Soon after the advertised time for com- mencement the teams appeared on the field, and C. Anderton was deputed to start the game on behalf of , the Free Wanderers. From a scrimmage formed here, Le Peton passed to Hindle, that player taking operations, to the Warrington twenty-five. Barnes here mulled a pass from Warren, but the home team forwards made up for this by a neat dribble to centre, in which Ashton and, W. Dillon were prominent. The Warringtonians then bore down on the visitors' citadel, Speakman getting over, but the bell was ruled dead. C. Anderton dropped, out, but the home team kept up the attack, and pressed the visitors back on their lines. The Wanderers rallied and relieved to centre. Rigby and Warren next headed a good rush, Le Peton saving in good style. Povey was most conspicuous by a splendid dribble from half-way close to the visitors' lines. Exchange kicking by Hindle and Massey was next witnessed, play finally settling in the Free Wanderers' territory. The leather was taken over the line, Dreschfeld saving by kicking dead. An- derton again dropped out, Barnes returning in fine style in touch at quarter-flag, and from a series of scrim- mages formed in close proximity to the Wanderers' goal, Speakman gave Barnes a chance, but that player trans- ferred to Jolley, who brushed aside all opposition, and scored the first try for the home team. The place was in a favourable position, but Barnes failed to increase its value. Anderton re-started, no return being made. Barnes shortly afterwards made his mark at half-way, and Frank Turner was entrusted with the place, a splendid bid for goal being made, the ball only falling short by a few feet. The visitors' forwards, headed by Anderton and Johnson, started a pretty movement, but danger was averted by Buxton kicking into touch at half way, and a neat dribble by Jolley and Frank Turner took the leather back. Jolley tridd hard to get away, but was well tackled by Le Peton. Half-time was called with the score—Warrington 1 try and 2 minors to Free Wanderers nil. Frank Turner re-commenced operations, the home team taking play in the Wanderers' territory. Dreschfeld tried hard to break through the Warrington defence, but he was well tackled by Jolley. Le Peton here stopped a dangerous rush of the home team but a good kick by Massey sent . the oval over the line, G. Anderton touching down. C. Anderton dropped out, and a neat dribble by the visiting forwards took operations to centre field. Hindle next made his mark, and punted to the home side quarter flag. A good run by Jolley and pass to Barnes transferred the game to their opponents' end, and from some loose play Warren gained possession and passed splendidly to Barnes' the latter player dropping a neat goal. C. Anderton started, from the centre, and Barnes was again to the fore by: one of his dodgy runs to half-way. Warrington maintained a supremacy during the rest of the game, which ended with the score : Warrington, one goal, three minors, to Free Wanderers nil. The game was sadly interfered with owing to the inclement state of the weather, and it as very difficult for the backs to hold the ball when it came in their way. To the Warrington backs too much praise cannot e awarded—Warren for his Unselfish play, his passing b leaving nothing to be desired. His companion Speak- man played with all his old fire and dash. The three- quarters played a grand combined game, and it is a re- markable feature that the trio of fixtures that have al- ready been played, not only have they been won, but a dropped goal has been included in the score on each oc- casion. Each of the three-quarters has had a share in them, viz., Massey against Aspull, Jolley in the Barrow match, and finally Barnes in this encounter. Buxton was safe, and of the forwards Povey, Frank Turner, and Ashton deserve special mention. On the Free Wan- derers' side Allen was the shining light, and Le Peton worked hard, but his off-side play sadly spoiled what- ever notice he merited. Of the forwards' Anderton and Dreschfeld were always in the thick. The following were the teams :—Warrington—Filll back, Buxton

three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes (captain), Massey; half backs, W. Speakman, Warren; forwards, J. Craghan, E. Dillon, Ashton, Frank Turner, Povey, Da- vies, Rigby, W. Dillon, W. Hayes. Free Wanderers— Full back, G. Anderton ; three-quarter backs, E. Allen, J. Worthington, and T. Hindle; half backs E. A. Le Peton and J: Oswald; forwards, C. AndertOn, E. Mc- Lewn, W. Scholfield, Dreschfeld, F. Walker, D. John- son, E. Bristow-e, E. Hebden, and J. Dewse. Referee: Mr. Walmsley, " Football Times."
