The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 52 cases, 12 of which were new and 40 old cases.—On the motion of Mr. BLACICIIIIRST, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY, the minutes were passed.

rita COnPORATION CRITICISED. . Mr. JOLLEY called attention to the fact that as he was . coming along Guardian-street to that meeting there were 16 or 18 tubs on the footpath. He would not have mentioned the matter if it had not been that there was present a member of the Corportion Sanitary Commit- tee, and he hoped also that the reporters, would take notice of it. These tubs were perhaps more offensiye to the eye than to the nose, but at the same time he thought it was,a, very improper thing to have these tubs, along two-thirds of the street. Such a thing would not' be done in Bridge-street. He did not know whether they ' had been put there to let the Guardians see what the Corporation could do or not, but he objected to the tubs being there near mid-day. He hoped the Board would express its opinion so that the Corporation would see that cottagers, and even a Board of Guardians should not be offended unnecessarily. The Corporation Should not do hi Guardian-street what they would not do in Bridge-street.—Mr. Isstsstwoon : Or Palmyra-square.— MR. JOLLEY : Yes, or Palmyra-square.—Mr. RATCLIFFE : What about the stir-pots. (Laughter.)—Mn. Jor,,Lvy did not want to say anything unkind, but he hoped such a thing would not happen again. MR. ISHERWOOD said he had got a letter from the Town Clerk to say these things were not a nuisance.—Mr. GRF.ENING said he was the member of the Sanitary Committee referred to. He quite agreed with Mr. Jolley if those tubs were never seen, and he would also be 've7, glad if all the arrangements of the Sani- tary Comildtted could be carried on without smell, but it was not .quite practicable. The occurrence did not take place in Guardian-street alone for opposite his (Mr. Greenhig's) house in Bewsey-roaci, he had seen eight or ten tubs, all in a row. If they could send a member • of the Sanitary Committee round with every gang of men perhaps those things would not occur, but they had to trust to themen who did the work. The nuisance from . the tubs was not much to be complained of if there was , no smell from the matter in them.—The CHAIRMAN said he did not see the tubs when he came, and they were not , there when Mr. Voisey name in rather late. He did not I think the Sanitary Committee were to blame, and he did 6 not think that if they had any choice they would choose , Guardian-street on the occasion when the Guardians were to meet. The observations that had been made , would draw attention to the matters and if anything could be done they would have the desired effect.—Mr. Ismeawoon said he had it on the authority of the Town , Clerk three months after he (Mr. Isherwood) wrote to ; him, that there was no smell. The matter then • d9pped. APPOINTMENT OF NURSE.
Miss Harper, of Bootle, who was in attendance on the Gruardians,-was appointed nurse to the Workhouse Hospital. _
TUE GUARDIANS AND VACCINATION.

• Mr. CrAmu, in moving his motion, that the word " de- i termined " should be left out of a placard issued by the Guardians with regard to vaccination, said that no doubt 20 years ago the Warrington Guardians would naturally be aetermmea to enforce the Vaccination Acts, believing them to be beneficial to the masses of the people, and a preventive in cases of small-ox, but that idea to-day was not tolerated. There were very few individuals who believed that vaccination did prevent small-pox, and the enforcement of these Acts was very' detrimental to the people. They found that the enforcement of the Acts pressed very heavily on poor pedple that could not afford to pay the penalties spoken of on the placard, and therefore these people had to submit to have their children vaccinated against their will. The result of this enforcement in a great many cases was disastrous. He found that a month since their clerk told them he had received several returns with regard to the work done by certain persons employed by them to enforce these acts. He said that the work was progressing satisfactorily, so far as he could say, but we did not hear those returns read. As far as he (Mr. Clarke) knew, they were not so satis- factory as they ought to be, or as that Board would wish them to be. They did not know by them what occurred throughout the Umon, but he knew personally about one part of the Union and could therefore speak for himself. He might refer them to a case which he visited in Wood street, Earlestown. The child's name was Alice Harris, and she was vaccinated on the 19th April last. Four weeks after she had been vaccinated he visited the child, and found that she had four large holes in the arm and an abscess under the arm. He visited her several times afterwards, and found her still suffering, but on the 29th September she died—to his mind, from the effects of vac- cination. The doctor did not certify that she had died from vaccination, and he considered that in such cases a proper investigation should take place—that was a coroner's inquest—when all particulars would be brought

out. Another case he might refer to occurred in the same street where he lived. A child named Charles Hughes, who was vaccinated on the 10th of August, took ill four days afterwards, and a few days later it was taken to be examined by the doctor. The doctor took some matter from it, then two children were Vaccinated Iwith the matter taken from the, sick . child, and it died during the same day. In this case also there was 'no certificate that the child had, died from the effects of vaccination. The certificate stated, "Died from teeth- ing, after three hours' convulsions." But it did not state what caused the convulsions, and he VMS afraid these were cases which ought tobeproperly investigated. There was another child he wished to refer to—John Gerrard, living in Sankey-street—who was not dead, but was still suffering. It was perfectly healthy at the end of six months, and then was vaccinated. Sometime afterwards it broke out all over with scabs, but these, after being doctored with for some weeks, disappeared. Some four or live weeks ago, however, it lost the we of its legs and the arm which was vaccinated. The child was still suffer- ing i , and he could not say whether t was mending or not; but, to all appearances, it was not likely to live. He could mention other cases which had suffered ex.' treinely, but he thought if the gentlemen forming that Board of Guardians knew the terrible agonies that mothers had .to endure through seeing their children suffer, they would not be so determined to enforce the Acts laid down. For his part, he was equally determined, on the other side, and, as an individual, he declined to enforce the Acts on others.—The proposition of Ma. Clarke's did not, however, find a seconder.—ln answer to Mr. Ratcliffe, the CIZRIE said that if the resolution was passed and-the-word- taken out;-the Guardians would be in exactly the same position as before with re- gard to the Vaccination Acts.—Mr. Voisey said if the metion had been discnssed, he was prepared to adduce statistics which he thought would have convinced the Guardians that there .was some efficacy in vaccination. —After a few more remarks the matter dropped, there not being a seconder for Mr. Clarke's proposition.

div.p: do not believe that the sound investing public. have de- sired that it should be continued; at all events this company declines to pay interest during construction. It is true they do not possess the power to do so, but there is no doubt that they could have obtained the nec,essary permission from Parliament had they .cared to do so. ,The directors had, however, a rooted objection to taking such a step, and the public will doubtless sup- pqrt them in their determination. further point of interest is that no "preference stock" can be issued to the prejudice of the ordinary shareholders and the debenture-stock which the Com- pany has the power to raise is to be reserved for what it is intended, viz., to equip the line, when it is made. It will, therefore, be seen that there is no probability of the present issue being " swamped" by prior claims on the part of holders of other classes of stocks. To enable the engineers.and other advisers of the directors to come to the conclusion they hate done upon these points they must of course have made every calculation that it is possible to make as to the probable ;cost of construction, &c., and it is satisfactory to find that they are prepared to so 'confidently stand by their estimates. . We have now touched upon what appear to us to be the most salient features of the prospectus. For any further information our readers may desire we must refer them to`the document itself and to the gentle- men whose names will be found at the foot of the pros- pectus. . .

CORRESPONDENCE. 'A letter to the Clerk- was read from Colonel Jones, stating that he was desired by the Local Governtnent Boundaries Commissioners to draw attention to the Act (Local 'Government Boundaries Act, 1887), a copy of which was enclosed, and to ask for any observations?. he (the Clerk) might be pleased to make with regard to the boundaries of the Union and County.—Another letter; also addressed to Mr. Sutton, was read from Mr. EL Bleckly; who stated that he was in communication with the newly-appointed Boundary Commissioners, and asked if there was any suggestion which occurred to him (Mr. Sutton) on the subject of the Warrington boundary spier as county government was concerned. The object „would be to make the geographical and the administra- tive boundaries conterminous. An ?Iteration as he (Mr. 'Bleckly) recollected was made some years ago. It would seem to him easier to retain a portion of Cheshire within Lancashire than, vice-versa.—The CLERK said that Mr. Bleckly's letter came to him at Harrogate, and he at once replied to it; of course dealing with the question from his own view Of its merits. Mr. Sutten then read his letter to Mr. Bleckly, which expressed opinions strongly averse, for reasons he assigned, to any interference with the present Union boundary. The chief of these reasons appeared to be the central position of Warrington, and of the Workhouse and Schools. He also pointed out that all the conditions under which the Cheshire town- ships were taken many years ago from the Runcorn Union and put to the Warrington Union would be reversed, whilst all that had been done because of that changer must • necessarily remain. In conclusion, he asked Mr. Bleckly to favour him with an interview upon the whole subject on his, return home.— Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that the clerk in his letterexpressed the opinion that there would be no advantage in chang- ing the borders of the Union as regards Cheshire. He (Mr. Darbyshire) wished it to be understood that that was the clerk's own opinion only,..and not the opinion of the Guardians.—The CLERK said that would be under- stood from the fact that he had written the letter before the 'Guardians met. He also- explained that in writing his letter he took the broad view of the whole Union, and did not write from the point of view of the Cheshire townships only.—ln answer to Mr. Voisey, Mr. DARBY- SHIRE said that Mr. Edward Greenall, who was the chief magistrate in their village, and a good many other rate- payers, were very wishful t 6 be transferred to the Run- corn Union, and they, had been asking him as the Guar- dian of the township why he did not move in the matter, and try to get them a change into the Runcorn Union. As far as he himself was concerned, he did not want a change. It was the ratepayers of Grappenhall who wanted the change, and wished to go in with the rest of the petty sessional division of Dare,sbury, which included Grappenhall and a large portion of Latchford. Mr. Sutton had suggested that there might be some division by the Ship Canal, and he did not wish to move in the matter seeing that the Ship Canal might change the boundary.—Mr. VOISEY asked if Mr. Darbyshire could I give some reasons why the ratepayers Of Grappenhall wished for a change.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said the main reason was that they would not be rated so heavily. ' ,(Laughter.)—Mr. BiAciumnsr And a very proper ,reason, too.—Mr. RATCLIFFE : They would not have to pay so much to the Warrington poor; it is the dark blot on the Union is Warrington.—The CHAIRMAN said that no doubt when the queition did come ui) it would be dealt with on very broad grouncts indeed.—Mr. JOLLEY said although he was slightly in, terested in Grappenhall he should be entirely opposed to any change.—Mr. BLACKIitusT said that when the question eventually came before the public the people who wished for a change would tell them that they had other reasons for the change besides pounds, shillings, and pence.— Mr. VOISEY asked Mr. Blackhurst to give those other reasons, but Mr. BLACKHURST replied that he was not prepared to give the reasons, but he knew there were reasons.—lt was then agreed that each member of the Board should be supplied with a copy of the correspon- dence and 'with a copyk of the Boundaries Act, in order that the whole subject might be discussed at a future meeting. .
APPLICATION FOR INCREASE. A letter was read from Mr. H. Houghton, egilector, Newton, for an increase of his salary of £9O a's7ear. The matter was referred to the Newton Committee.
MEMORIALS.

The CLERK submitted memorials from the Darlington and Merthyr Tydvil Boards of Guardians in favour of Boards of Guardians being granted power to reduce the salaries of their officers without the consent of the Local Government Board.—After a short discussion, Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved that the memorials be signed on be- half of the poard, but it was Ultimately agreed that the matter should be left over till next meeting. The Chairman having reported as to the proceedings of the recent Poor Law Conference at iklanchester, the relief cases were proceeded with. . •

div.head: DEATH FROM LOCKJAW.
div.p: THE DEATH FROM LOCKJAW.

lOn Monday, Mr. Brighouse', coroner, held an ad- journed- inquest at the Workhouse, Warrington, as to the death of an Irish labourer, 60 years of age, named Thomas Loftus. Deceased Was a fiirm laz bourer, and had been engaged, on the 21st ult., by ' Mr. Clarke, of Sevenoaks, Great Budworth, to work jat a steam threshing machine. After the threshing machine iiiid completed its work it was being taken to a neighbouring smithy for repairs, and several labourers jumped on to it for a "lift." Loftus, in i attempting to get on, fell upon the road, and was in- jured in the right hand and leg by a wheel of the , thresher. The man was conveyed to Warrington Infirmary, where his wounds were dressed, and he was then sent to the Workhouse Hospital, where he ultimately died of lockjaw. At the previous in- quest a suggestion was made that the deceased had,been knocked down by another labourer named Daniel Higgins, and the inquest was adJourned that Higgins might be brought forward, but it was stated by Police-Inspector Spinks that the police had not i been able to discover Higgins. The first witness ' I recalled was Thos. Loftus, nephew of the deceased, who said he had nothing further to add to the evidence he gave at the previous inquiry'.—Henry- Williamson, threshing machine owner, of Whitley Inferior, was next called, and' stated that he was in charge of the machine on the day of the accident. . After the accident he stopped the machine, and, getting off, he saw deceased with his hand bleeding and walking lame. He told deceased that he had no business to get on the machine, and the latter replied, "It's my own fault; I have none to blame 'only myself." Witness was cross-examined as to his knowledge of the deceased and Higgins, and he gave his answers in a very cautious and hesitating manner. One of the, jurymen remarked that he seemed 'to have a remarkable failing of memory.—The Coroner said they must all feel that if witness had taxed his memory he would have been able to say more.—Evidence' was next given by William Clarke, farmer, Senna Green," Seven- oaks, and Michael Graham, an Irish labourer. This , latter witness said that he was sitting on the machine when deceased tried to get on. He did not see Higgins push deceased, and he believed that if Higgins had attempted to make room for Loftus he would ha,ve endangered his own position. After the accident, deceased said to Higgins, "I will not ilaccept your assistance; it was your fault ;" and when they were driving him to the Warrington In- firmary they passed Higgins on the way, and the deceased shook his hand at him and said "It is youi. fault," No one had a right to sit on the ma- chine, and they had been told before by Williamson 'not to get on to it. Dennis Miller, labourer, Great Budworth, and John Frith, farmer, Sevenoaks likewise gave evidence. Mr. Frith, it was stated, 'had driven,Loftus labia own trap to the warring- ton'lnfirmary, a distance of about eight miles, and the Coroner complimented him On Ins kindnesS.— , Inspector Spinks .deposed that 'deceased made a f statement before his death, in which he said. he I belonged to County Mayo, Ireland, where he-had a • wife and six little children. He did not blame anyone for the accident that had befallen him.—Dr. ' Spilka next testified as to the cause of death, and after the Coroner had summed up, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." A juror remarked that they quite agreed with the Coroner's remarks as ' •to Williamson's evidence.—The Coroner; He raised suspicion in our mind when there was no.necessity i for it.

_ A WORD ABOUT PROTECTION. Sir,—The Earl of Dunraven, in his recent speech at the PUblic Hall, advocated, in a certain sense, the return to Protection. I should be pleased if any of your readers could tell me in what way the application of protective duties would benefit the nation at large. Certainly some individuals would benefit most strongly by a duty upon German and Belgian iron, but would the people derive any advantage? I think not. As a matter of fact, they would have to pay far more for manufac- tured iron than they do at the present time, and I think no Government should fill the pockets of a few manu- facturers, while they are at the same time robbing the working-man. Fair Traders say, " Oh, but the working- man's wages will be increased." Certainly they will, but he will have to pay a corresponding amount more for his food and necessaries of life. And then with regard to the sugar bounties. What does it matter to us if the French are fools enough to pay for our sugar, as they do? Our sugar refineries were closed, or almost so, and some hundreds of working- men were thrown out of employment. But is not that a small matter in the face of the fact that the whole popu- lation of Great Britain and Ireland can buy their sugar far cheaper, and all because the French nation are taxed tokay bounties to the sugar manufacturers in France? Then' Protectionists say" If we do put a tax upon corn imported from Russia and America, India can throw more land into the cultivation of wheat, and so supply us with all we need." This is all right so far as it goes. But in the event of war, what will happen? These vessels laden with corn would be captured by the enemy, or else we should have to keep our whole fleet employed in protecting them while; if the corn came from America, which would be a neutral power, the ships could traverse the seas without fear. I should be pleased if any Protectionist would inform me of any method he would employ to get over this last difficulty.—Yours truly,
Warrington, October October 12th, 1887.

EMIGRATION v. IMMIGRATION. Sir,—A very serious question for the English working- man is slowly, yet surely, coming to the front in the one of emigration. We may daily with these burning ques- tion, and refuse to apply radical remedies, but the day is not far distant when the cry of the unemployed will extend itself right through the winter months into the sunshine of summer; and, then, woe unto those who have neglected the appeal of the distressed. Each one of our eminent statesmen has, in his turn, told us of the capabilities of the land. Often has it been pointed out to us that, with respect to population, Great Britain need not fear for years to come any scarcity in her own resources for producing ample supplies of food products. What, then, can. be the reason for the yearly exodus that is going on? In 1886, the total number of emigrants who left our shores, of British and Irish origin, was 232,900. In 1885, the figures were 207,644, an increase of 25,256. It is to be borne in mind that these emigrants represent the best in physique amorigst our farming and artisan population. Already doleful statements are ap- pearing wherein the degeneracy of the race is depicted. Army standards are lowered, and in Ireland it is stated that there will soon be none left but the old and de-

crepid. Should Englishmen neglect for a few years longer to deal with the matters to which I have repeatedly drawn i attention in your paper, viz.. all that is included n what is called the land question as rent and royalities, will undoubtedly be lost. and will yield a profit to the worker, and to him only. Landlords must stand on one side; the welfare of the nation demands it. Men and women of all grades are being driven from our shores. Educated lads are taking the places of edu- cated, but costly, men. The son is displacing the father, and, with the help of automatic machinery, is driving art and skill to the wall. Hence the year's increase in our emigration figures. But, sir, it is found that with all our emigration , state aided or society aided, our population in England gets no less. Lord Brabazon recently re- marked, "it is useless to pump a ship when the water pours in equally fast through the leak." It is esamated that a most undesirable class of immigrants are pouring into London at the rate of 1,000 a week. The Chinese would have done for our colonies what the German, the Pole, the Russian, and the Jews are doing ' for England, but they were stopped. England has always been a home for the foreign patriot, but I know of no reason why it should be the home of the dirty underselling German, or the Polish Jew. To come amongst us is a very different thing, from us go- ing amongst them. Wherever an Englishman goes he takes a loftier perception of life, and its duties. As a rule he is the leaven that leavens the whole, but the na- tionalities now forming colonies in London, Manchester, Liverpool, and, indeed, all our great towns, are blindly dragging us down to the lowest depths of continental life. Education on the continent, in spite of all the glowing statements I have at various times given of it, seems to aim at nothing higher than the creation of a keen, sel- fish, and competing race. It does more than this, by its selection of picked men for the army, custom house, excise, the police, and municipal guards. It leaves, as the "New York Herald" recently said, a deformed, rickety, dirty, wretched, and thievish lot to swell the ranks of other lands. In an emigration report recently issued, One agent stated he had returned 997 immigrants to the country from which he came. Of the number 70 were insane, 20 were idiots, 10 convicts, 300 suffering from disease; the rest were blind and paupers. Sir, are Englishmen to be driven from the home country to make room for these? Is it wise of English working-men to be fighting landlords' battles in Ireland, while they themselves are being supplemented by such as the above? Is England to be the rubbish heap of the Continent? "What had been the effects of this immigration? In the sweating tailor trade men were receiving as little as Is. and women 10d. per day. Half a day's work was reckoned at eight hours. Could they wonder, when ladies' aprons were made at 5Ad. per dozen; slippers at 3d. per pair, and knickerbockers for Is. 9d. per dozen, at the shame and misery that followed? Could they wonder with such wages paid that there was an army of unsexed creatures ? " It is, as Carlyle said, "England is full of wealth, yet England is dying of inanition." It may be that my next letter which appears in the " Examiner " will be from practical experience gained as an emigrant, so I beg for a little extra space. There FAX= to be an impression that the present generation are better off than were their forefathers, and I have had to submit at various times that this was not so. The hurry-scurry of life, and its responsibilities must be considered. Once, to be ignorant was bliss; this is all altered. Slavish, cringing poverty, bowing and scraping before the parson and the squire did, in the old times, obtain in the country districts, but the yokel has no responsibilities. The squire has, by the aid of landlord- made laws, cleared his land of paupers, and large towns are the result. Labour saving machines are gradually destroying all labour, but at what cost? Cheap produc- tion is only another phrase for creation of millionaires. Yes,wealthy manufacturers, squires, and parsons quietly hob-nob in their sylvan retreats, while we, denizens of the slums and alleys, vainly cry out for help in our meliorating schemes. How wise these gentry would be if they would only give such pacifying sops as Free Lending Libraries, Free Baths, and Recreation Grounds. Do they know what is going on in our large towns? I often wonder do they ever throw the novel on one side, and read the people's literature; for instance, the follow- ing, a result of immigration "If the facts and tricks of the sweaters were known, the Government ought to make a clean sweep of the system at once, and thus protect their subjects. There are already in London 120,0000 Sweaters' Victims, all working in miserable dens, for very long hours, and for very low wages. A few facts will suffice to illustrate the evils of the system, and arouse the righteous indig- nation of our readers. In the New-road, Whitechapel, there is a "den" which is very small, and there are no fewer than 12 persons at work, with a large coke fire and seven gas-lights. The hours of labour for both sexes are from 15 to 18 hours per day, arid the average wage of the men for the 18 hours is 25., for the women 9d., that is 10. and id. respectively. In Old Montague-street, E., there is a workshop, the size of which is only 8 feet square, in which there are 10 hands at work, with a coke fire and six gas-lights. The hours of labour are for men 16, for women 14, with a wage of na. for the 14 hours. In Cannon-street-road, E., is a workshop 14 feet square, with 20 hands—men, women, and children —working; there is a large coke fire, and there are 12 gas-lights. The hours of labour for men are 15, with the average wage of 2s. id. per day. The women work 14 hours for an average wage of 60. per day." We are now receiving the benefits of a government pledged to economy.. I wonder do your Tory readers guess how it is working the problem out? By a system of contract, and sub-contract, thrice repeated, they will be enabled to boast of the large amount of money saved to the country. Will they also boast that their sub- contractors are largely employing foreign immigrants. Will they state that England's daughters are being Un- sexed so that we may have economy And that our sisters flock to Regent-street to add to their weekly earn- ings ? No, lam afraid not, and so the game will go on. No doubt there is a lot of pessimism in these state- ments, but without doubt they are founded on diligent research, prompted by an earnest desire to see my fel- low workers partake of their share of the good things that abound, but which are monopolised by the few. Co-operation is the secret to be grappled with by work- ers, but not co-operation for mere " divi." " Divi" is only another word for selfishness, and will never help on Internationalism. We must strive to attain the latter, or the day when the ploughshare will take the place of the sword is far distant. October 15th, 1887.
CLIFFORD DIX.

RUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday after- noon. There were present (Colonel Ashton) chair- man), Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, add J. Lockwood; Messrs-. Taylor, Brandreth, Parr, Hadfield, Kirkham, and H. Linaker (clerk.) COMPLIMENTARY TO TICE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.-A letter was read from the Local Government Board, sug- gesting that the Authority should make fresh regulations with regard to dairies, cowsheds, Izc. which would be free from the objections previously Made by the Local Government Board.—Mr. Hadfield said the Authority had sent regulations up to the Local Government Board, and it was about seven or eight months before they an- swerecL As the regulations came into force after one month if there was anything wrong in them it was due to the carelessness and stupidity of the Local Govern- ment Board themselves. Besides, the recommendations the Local Government Board made were so absurd that they were hardly worth discussing. He proposed that the letter from the Local Government Board should lie on the table, but that the Authority purchase a couple of the bye-laws suggested as models by the Local Govern- ment Board.—Mr. Aaron seconded this proposal.—Mr. Mclntyre thought there were gentlemen in Cheshire that knew °far better what was requisite for cattle and dairy sheds than the Local Government Board. He thought what the Local Government Board wrote before was sufficient evidence that they were not competent for framing rules for the erection of farm buildings. Mr. Hadfield said the person who wrote did not know what he was writing about.—Mr. Parr: I should think the fellow had never been in a cowshed in his life who said that 800 cubic feet of air was necessary for each cow. How would the animals go on in the dead of winter with that space P—Mr. Aaron: They would want stoves. (Laughter.)—Mr. Hadfield's proposition was then agreed to. _ . .

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORt. - Dr. Adams (medical officer of health), reported that during the quarter end- ing September 30th, the registered returns record 138 births and 85 deaths in the four registration sub-districts of the Authority's district. Of the births, 57 were males and 81 females. The birth rate was 27.6 per 1,000 per annum as compared with 30.8 in the corresponding quarter of 1886. Only two deaths had occurred from the greater zymotic diseases, viz., one from measles and one from typhoid fever (the latter being imported) while cancer accounted for 9 deaths, and no less than 13 deaths formed subjects for coroner's inquests, two only of which were not due to violence or injury. OuTrinamc OF DISEASE.-Mr. Farrington (the inspec- tor) said that as he had been away since the last meet- ing and had only returned to the district the previous day, he had not much to report. He had been informed however, that there had been an outbreak of measles land fever at Weston. He was also told that a death had taken place that morning at Weston Village.—The Chairman: There has been a death from typhoid at Runcorn.—Mr. Farrington: I believe so. He also men- tioned that the school at Aston had been closed on ac- count of measles. There were, however, not many cases.—lt was agreed, on the suggestion of Mr. Aaron, that the Medical Officer should be asked to visit the closed schools. _ . .
This was all the business of public interest.
THE RIVAL BILLPOSTERS AT sr. HELENS.

At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Friday, before Alderman j. Harrison and Alderman J. C. Gamble. Nathaniel Edwards, of the firm of Messrs. Abbot and Co., bill-posters, and his two brothers, John Wilson Edwards, and Thomas Edwards, were charged with assaulting Thomas Campbell, a bill-poster, in the employ of Mr. W. G. Deacle, and there was a cross- summons against Campbell for assaulting Nathaniel Edwards. Mr. J. P. Mearns appeared for the prose- cution, and Mr. H. L. Riley defended the brothers Edwards.—Mr. Mearns said he appeared to prosecute the three defendants on a charge of malicious, brutal, and cowardly assault. Although there had been numer- ous differences between the masters before, he did not intend to introduce them into the matter. That wasacase in which it was not an illiterate man who was guilty of the offence. Nathaniel Edwards was not an illiterate than and if he thought the prosecutor was trespassing he had a remedy without using violence.—Benjamin W. Leach said he was agent for the property which was for sale at the corner of Hardshaw and Claughton-streets, and Campbell had received the general instructions given re- specting posting bills on the property for sale. In answer to Mr. Riley, witness said they did not generally ask the tenant's leave to post bills on the property.— Thomas Campbell said he was a bill-poster in the em- ploy of Mr. Deacle. On the sth instant he had received certain bills to post on Claughton Chambers, one on the front in Flardshaw-street, one at the corner in Claugh- ton-street, and one on Messrs. Abbot's establishment. He was proceeding to post the bill on Abbot's place, having posted the others all right, and had got up ten steps on his ladder when Nathaniel Edwards pulled him down and threw him on the ground, and then fell with his knees on his (Campbell's) chest, and defendant's brothers urged him to "kill the ." They said he was the man they wanted to thump many a time. He was kicked, his left eye had been injured, and he be- lieved Nathaniel had bitten him. In consequence of the injuries he had received he had not been able to follow his work since, and Mr. beaele had been obliged to employ another man in his place.— Frederick Wilson, E. Budding, George Barton, jun., Thomas Casey, and Mrs. Kendrick gave corroborative evidence.—Police-constable Bramwell stated that he saw a crowd, and found the defendant, Nathaniel Edwards, upon the complainant. He took him off , and said hewould have to gb with him to the police office.—Mr, Riley said the first submission which would almost be expected from him, was that against the two defendants, other than Nathanial, there was no case.—The magistrates Concurred, and dismissed them.—Mr. Riley then ad- dressed the Bench on behalf of Nathanial Edwards, and contended that magistrates could not try eases in which a question of title was involved. He submitted with confidence that the whole basis of that case was a ques- tion of title.—Mr.Mearns said the proper time for thatto be brought up was before he had called his witnesses.— Campbell, who was recalled, said he did not place his ladder against Abbot's property, and he did not intend to put the bill anywhere than on the property for sale, which adjoined defendant's office.—Nathaniel Edwards was called and said complainant came into Claughtou- steeet, on Wednesday afternoon, and raised his ladder against his (Edward's) p'remises, and he said to him, "Don't put it there, put it on the other side of the spout where there is a much better position for it," and he answered "I am going to put it here." He then said, "If you do persist in posting it there I'll pull the ladder from under you."—Mr. Riley said if a man believed the property to be his he was justified according to law in resisting trespass upon it.—The Magistrates said they would ,djourn the case till Tuesday when they would hear the evidence in full, and then send the case to the Quarter Sessions. They considered that excessive vio- lence had been used towards Campbell.—After luncheon, Mr. Riley said Mr. Edwards was willing that he should withdraw the point of title and let the case proceed on its merits.—Edwards then gave evidence as to the al- leged assault made on him by Campbell, which was cor- roborated by a young man named Grey, who admitted in cross-examination that he had come from Widnes along with Edwards' brothers.—The Chairman said the case against Campbell would be dismissed, and as Edwards's case was one of very serious assault they would fine him £.5 including costs, the greatest penalty they could inflict. MANCHESTER MAY AND STRAW, FRIDAY.-Hay, 6d. to 7d; clover, 7d. to Bd. ; wheat straw, at to 5d ; oat straw, tlid. to sd. per Stone of 14115. MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. - The tone is steady all round and a moderate trade doing in some departments. The increasing stiffness in Liverpool does not seem to be giving much assistance ' to. spinners. Cloth is not active, but a moderate trade is reported in China shirtings. India makei are quieter. Good printers ars steady, with a fair business, but Burnley qualities are less active. Mexicans keep very poor, and heavy goods move with great deliberation. LIVERPOOL PROVISION, FRIDAY. - Beef rules quiet and has declined in value. Pork is slow of sale, buyers being cautious. Prices of bacon show no quotable alteration from i Those current yesterday, with the exception of backs and bel- lies, former rates for which are barely maintained. Hams ex- perience a good inquiry for fresh landed parcels. Shoulders remain steady. Cheese closes quiet. Butter is without alter- ation. LONDON PRODUCE, FRIDAY.-The sugar market continues quiet; German beetroot quoted at 12s. lid. November-Decem- ber. Coffee without change. Tea: 670 packages China and Indian and Ceylon advertised for sale to-day. Rice ex- tremely quiet. Cotton market inactive. Jute steady and more doing. Tallow, Y.C., 325. spot. Turpentine, 265. 3d. This Company was promoted antithe Special Acts obtained by manufacturers and traders in ,-St, Helens and the neigh- bourhood for the purpose of more thoroughly providing railway accommodation for theonormous and rapidly increasing traffic of this populous commercial distriet. The Railway consists of two sectionslB-miles long, commen- cing at Lowton, on the Manchester, iiheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway system, and ending on, thetCheithire Lines Railway at the north end of Liverpool. The map of the district (which can •be obtained on applica- tion to the Secretary) ohows that the-railway- will form a valu- able through line in the Nery heart ofone of the most exten- sive coal-producing andtmffic-bearing districts of Lancashire, the large and important manufacturing town of St. Helens being the central point of the --system, and by means of the Railway St. Helens and the surrounding districts will be brought into direct communication wititLiverpool, Southport, and Preston in one dlreettion, and Avileh Manchester, Wigan, : and the Districts sereed by .the Mandiester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire,/the Great Northern, mut the Midland Railways and the Cheshire Lines Railway in. theether. St. Helens has a pop-station of 60,00Ginhabltants, which is rapidly increasing. The town contains thedarged glass manu- factories in the world, and has ,extensive alkali and copper sworks, besides collieries, ironfoundries„,and•engineering estab- r ilshments. The'Directors have fittle,doubt:thatairery large there of the traffic of the town, and in particular that ,between St. Helens ..and the Liverpool Docks (as .being the nearest and most °olive- :tient route), will pass owerithe new railway. The gross traffic of the St. Helens district is estimated to .amount to 4,000,000 tons per .annum or. thereabouts, and forms ore-eighth part of the mketedonnage of tianlnntlon and North- Western Railway Company. addition, however, tot be important tniffic from St.Holens, Use Company will secure aisige .trade.in .the other districts t-ough which the railway passes, which moontain collieries, adds, and manufactories of every kind. Ahe important collieries of Messrs. Riehare.Evans and Com- pany, with an annual output of 1,500,000 tone, are on the rail- Ws3, . and will be connected therewith. Thetailway also passes tins:ugh a large undeveloped evaltieldoa portion of which has sines the powers for the construction of this.tailway were ob- taintd been leased, and collieries are about tote established to work the same. These collieries will, it is estimated, have an outprt of of 250,000 tons par num, and ortill be connected with this railway. By. means of its connection with the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway wvatem, anew route *lll be provided to the, East Coast ports, full and Grirashyowith which at present St. Helens has no direct communication. The Directors have carefully -considered the question of en- teringinto arrangements with neighbouring Companies for the working of their Railway. They bare decidedito enter into no sucharmngements at present. They are confident that, constructed in an economical rnanner at cash prices, and manageti.on business principles, this line will show, as other lines made through populous tonal:mettle-1 localities have done, very 'satisfactory results. The average earnings over the whole of the systems, inclu- ding branch lines of the Lancashire and Yorkshise Railway, are £145. joer mile per week, the London and North-Western, £lOO, the Midland £lO2, and the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshise, £llO. It is well known that there sae certain sections of ittiese railways where the traffic shows a consider- ably higher result. Assuming that the earnings of the St. „Helens line commence at £7O per utile per week, and increase tlo £lOO per mile per week, the working expenses heino esti- 'mated at 55 per cent., and afterwards at 50 per cerk,, of the „ssross receipts, the net earnings would show an annual return ,upon the authorised Share Capital of 51- per cent. rising ,atortly to 7i. per cent. The Directors diave not paid any promotion money, nor do :they propose to pay interest during construction out of I :CAPRaI. The contract for the execution of the works has been let to Messrs. S. W. Pilling and Company, of Manchester, who un- dertske to construct the Railway by the 31st December, 1889, to the satisfaction ef the Board of Trade, and to maintain the came.for twelve months after the opening for public traffic. The Directors have carefully considered the necessary expenditure, and lxi'leve that the present issue of shares will amply cover the cost of the construction of the Railway and all other out- lay. The Directors have in the contract reserved the right to eon- structtlw Railway in two sections-namely, the section from St. Jielens to Lowton, and the section from St. Helens to Liver- pool. The Board will endeavour to arrange that one or other of these sections shall be completed as quickly as possible, so that a portion of the railway shall be eayning a revenue at an early date. ' No Preference Stock or Shares can be issued in priority to the Ordinary Shares without the assent of Parliament, and also the Shareholders; nor will any such issue be, in the Diree- tors' opinion, necessary. The Company havelpower to borrow on Debentures £183,000, but the Directors will advise that these Debentures be reserved to provide for the equipment and working of the railway when completed. BOROUGH OF ST. 'IDILENS. TO THE ELECTORS OF HARDSHAW WARD. LAIIIES &NB GENTIwEMEN,—The period for which you elected me will expire at the end of the present month. .li3 one of your representatives in the Town Council, I have endeavouretito advance, the interests oftthe town by advocat- ing and voting for such proposals that seemed likely to pro- I date the greatest prosperity at the least advance. Et has been my pleasured.° confer with a large number of ratepayers at..various times on important matters before the Council, to meat you in ptiblic assembly each year to give an amount of Whathes been dane in the past, and to learn your views as to the future, and, to attend over 300 meetings \ln evmmittee and •Cournill in order to give effect to your The work,done in the various committees of which I have been a member, as I think been fairly meltable. The gas department having made extensive enlargements and improvemente,'wlll beanie, when the plant is in full work, to reduce the prise of gas, and yet head over a balance to re- llevelhe genemlmtes, whilelhe lighting of the borough has been esonsidembly proved. The water supply will be ample for many years .when the new works are finished, espeektlly if sometaing is done to malve +be water frone Collins Green more suitable for domestic In the health department useful work has been done under great difficulties in anonuection with the scavenging of the town, but this matter is now In a fair way to bevheapened and made less objectionabla. being deeply interested in maintaining the present educa- tional arrangements of St. Helens, I have closely followed their worlfibig and have assisted in the schools aoranaittee to make its wark as usefulas possible. The settlement of the police questien is generally accepted as a step in the right direction, and already there are signs that the Chief Constableand his force will render efficient and valuable help to the other departments of the Corporation, and , thus improve the entire management, while the cost for a ' larger force than before will not be any higher, after the initial -expenses are paid in the first yeat's working. In offering my services far another term, in respmese to a requisition signed by a large number of ratepayers in the ward, I do so with a fa' sense of tile respoasilidlity resting capon a member of the Town Council, and if it be your pleasure to re- elect me as one et your representatives, I sball give my most earnest and careful attention to all matters relating to the I prosperity of the town at large, and my native ward in par- ticular. The necessity of creating more wards in the borough and hav- ing additional members of the COCilleil is in my view, both im- portant and urgent. The town has increased so much in its population, rateable value, and melamine estates, that its busi- ness demands more time and attention than can be fairly ren- dered by the small number of members at presenteonstltuting the CounelL There is also great need of a re-arrangement of committees, so that each department, with its offietats, may be under proper control and made to yield better results than at present, and the latter should not in any opinion be allowed to do other than corporation business. My views about the intercepting sewer, district bathe, and libraries are known to you, and will have my best attention when brought forward. Thanking you for the valuable help you have always been willing to give me in the discharge of my duty, and soliciting a continuance of your support, I have the honour to be, Ladies and gentlemen, Your obedient servant, JOHN FORSTER. 21, Hall-street, St. Helens, October fitti, 1887.

, ,allowed the expenditure to exceed the estimates ought IF3 'lto come before the Council again with a supplementary' md estimath. (Hear hear.) That appeared to him to be 1..1 the only efficient manner in which they could control 1 the expenditure. He had 17 or 18 years' experience Of. the Council, and he know pretty much how the thing was done. They might pass whatever resolutions they liked, but they would not have the slightest effect upon such men as Mr. John Burgess, because he had a NAT which he would ride to'death, and he was making the town pay very smartly for it. He thought some check I ought to be put, not only on the Sanitary, but upon ; every other Committee,—The Casiaxeit said that could only be done by getting'thembers of their Asaneiation on the Committees. A Sub-Committee,, consisting of the President, Vice- President, and Messrs. Green, Thornton, and Wright, was appointed to consider as to the objects of the Asso, ciation, and this concluded the business. MEETING OB COMMITTEE. A meeting of the committee of the Ratepayers'. Aiseci- ation was held at the Blue Bell Inn, Horsemarket-street, on Wednesday evening. The vice-president, Mr. James Smethurst, presided; and there were also present Messrs. Si Roberts, J. Barker, J. Dobson, S. Davies, W. Perry, T. Jones, J. Shaw Green, N. B. Percival, S. Barlow, W. T. Skelton' '' J. McCollom, J. E. Wright, J. Toft, B. Thornton, et. Blackhurst, and H. J. Longton (hon. sec. pro.. feni.)—The Cntairmax, in a few opening remarks, said it was not the intention of that association to torn things the wrong side up in the town. Their idea was to send persons to the Town Council who would assist those who were there to do their utmost to curtail the rates and to lessen the burden of which they were now complaining. It would be an utter impossibility for them to put an end to the work that had been already done for the sanitary reform of the borough, and no gentleman Ithere would attempt to do it. What they wanted to do ' was to stop further expenditure. (Hear, hear.) Mr. LONGTON then read letters from Councillor Platt, Councillor H. Roberts, and Mr. G. Woods. IMr. Platt wrote that he understood he ' had been appointed chairman, but as he could not devote the necessary time to the office he would be glad if the committee would excuse his declining to accept the nomination.—The CHAIRMAN re- marked that he hoped they should be able to persuade Mr. Platt to accept the office. (Hear, hear.)—The mi- nutes of a sub-committee were read which suggested that the annual subscription for property owners and members of the committee should be 10s., and ss. - for property owners who are ordinary, members of the .IZom. 1 mittee. After some discussion, however, it was , decided that the original decision in favour of half-a-crown ri4b- -1 scription/should be upheld.—Mr. J. Shaw Green Was I elected secretary.; Messrs. J. E. Wright and W. Perry, ' auditors ; and Mr. H. J. Lengton' solicitor, of the asso- ciation.—The selection of candidates for the forthcornfiag ; municipal elections was next proceeded with, the result ; being that the following gentlemen were selected for ; nomination i—North-West Ward, Mr. G. Blackhurst ; , South-East Ward, Mr. J. Smethurst and Mr. N. B. Per- , cival ; North-East Ward, Mr. J. Shaw Green; South- West Wird, Councillors Wright and J. Pierpoint. With , regard to the Latchford Ward, it was decided that the 'following-gentlemen should be invited to stand in the lorder named, Mr. Daniel Jones, Mr. James Strange, and Mr. Hodgkinson.—A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close.

This curious book has been dramatised and placed upon the stage of New York, where an actor has made a great hit by doubling the parts. Now this has been done, the marvel isit was not thought of before. It is easy to imagine what a strong thing Mr. Irving could have made out of the nightmare- like fancy. I suppose we shall be having the play transplanted to London. Mr. Stevenson had no hand in the work of adaptation, though it was done with his consent. He himself was not sanguine of 811CC08£1, holding that the story is too ugly and re- pulsive to be placed upon the stage. The dramatists, taking note of this objection, have, I believe, en- deavoured to make the piece more acceptable by in- troducing some love scenes. Mr. Stevenson is ac- companied on his present visit to America by his wife, whom he found in the United States. She is a bright, capable little woman, hailing from Indianapolis.

In the next place the line appears to supply what must be a real want and necessity in a neighbourhood, the traffic of which is so great as to form one-eighth of the whole tonnage. of the London and North-Western Railway Company. It seems almost impossible to be- lieve that such a district shoukl have been left so long as this has been in the hands of one Railway Company, but nevertheless such is the fact, and the London and North- Western Railway company have at the present time an absolute monopoly of the carrying trade, not only of the town of St. Helens, with its 0,000 inhabitants, and its glass works, copper works, alkali works, and other gigantic industries, but of the various -other places through which this line passes. By means of the com- munications provided by this line the Great Northern, Midland, and Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railways will all be brought into direct communication with the district, and the new railway will therefore form a most important feeder to these systems, by en- abling them to tap the 4,000,000 tons of traffic which are said to annually pass over the St. Helens system. It does not, therefore, appear necessary to add anything further to show the desirability of such a line as the pre- sent, and regarding the matter from a shareholder's point of view, this seems to sum up the whole question,

because where there is a necessity for a line, there is sure to be the traffic which will provide the means of paying good and substantial dividends. The Directors, with a view of showing what this line may be expected to do in this respect? and comparing the probable returns with other lines of a similar charac- ter, and allowing liberally for working expenses, esti- mate that the shareholders may look to dividends of Si, rising shortly to 7 per cent: Passing to the other statements of the prospectus, it should be noted that no promotion-money has been paid, which is another reason for commending the undertak- ing to the favourable consideration of the public, be- cause it is well known how frequent it is for large sums to be squandered amongst gentlemen who are supposed to have rendered services which possess great value in their own opinion, but which are of little practical bene- fit to the Company. Upon all these sums of course divi- dends have to be earned, and it does not speak well for the future management of the concern that money should be paid away without a valuable equivalent be- ing received in return. It is satisfactory therefore to find that the directors can make such anZunqualified statement as they-do upon this subject. Again, no interest,is to be paid during construction. This, if not quite a new departure, is at all events a re- turn to a more wholesome practice which existed before the time when the market was overstocked with public companies. [FROM oun CAVE CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, B.C. The Stock Exchange has experienced another sharp fall in prices, the full effect of which has not yet been revealed. On Tuesday so disastrous was the fall in Americans and Mexicans that it was feared that at one time over twenty brokers would be declared defatilters. Already several are known and one anticipated the in- evitable that he announced himself as such a day before the time. The settlement which concludes to-&.y (Fri- day) will prove one of the most disastrous for many a day, and the fall in prices all round has been very severely felt. On Wednesday the Middlesex magis- trates granted a music hall licence to the Empire Theatre, which had the effect of sending down the priceS of Pavilion shares, and when the news became generally known some heavy selling took place. These shares have been artificially raised to a high premium, and, oti their merits, are certainly not worth more than par. Another company of a similar character has been artificially stimulated by the Metropolitan Music Mall Company. These shares have also gone down in spite of the fact that a quarter dividend of 20 per cent has recently been declared. As a matter of fact this dividend was announced without any audit by a professional man, and the directors have taken the re- sponsbility of declaring this dividend in face of the fact that the returns do not justify it. A meeting of shareholders of the La Trinidad, Limitedt one of the unfortunate mining companies of the Abbot- Page group, was held on Wednesday, when the share, holders resolved to find a further Z 250,000 to secure the property, as, in spite of the money already paid, the company have no title to the property, and are entirely dependent upon the goodwill of the original vendor. A company is about to 136 brought out to carry on the business of Rudge and Co., the well-known bicycle and • tricycle makers. The undertaking is a sound one, and the directors are respectable. • Investors would be well advised to hold on to their securities, and not be frightened into parting with them at the present juncture. Of course such things as Pavilions, Metropolitans, and similar shares, should not be held beyond the first favourable opportunity of getting out of them ; but railway and similar substan- tial dividend-earning stocks should be retained. The fall in Greeks, due to rigging of the market last week, has been recovered, but it is of too speculative a stock to be held in any large quantities. Thursday saw the markets even worse than on Tuesday, and our advice to investors is to keep clear of speculation for the present.
